Wall Street Journal journalist Bojan Pancevski even claimed in a recently published book that a glamour model was among the yacht’s crew.
Moscow has dismissed the “Ukrainian frogmen” theory as fantasy, arguing that such a complex operation could not have been carried out in NATO-controlled waters by a small group without state assistance or Western intelligence involvement.
Zhuravlyov had previously evaded arrest. While living in Poland in 2024, he fled to Ukraine before he could be apprehended. Der Spiegel reported that he crossed the border in a vehicle belonging to the Ukrainian military attaché.
He later apparently returned to Poland and was detained there in September 2025. The following month, however, a Warsaw court rejected Berlin’s extradition request as “unfounded,” arguing that “blowing up critical infrastructure during a war… is not sabotage but denotes a military action.”
The September 2022 explosions severed three of the four Nord Stream pipelines built to carry Russian gas to Germany.
German authorities say the alleged team was led by Sergey K., identified by media as former Ukrainian special forces member Sergey Kuznetsov. He was arrested in Italy in August 2025 and extradited to Germany three months later.
Prosecutors charged Kuznetsov in June with “war crimes” for knowingly attacking civilian infrastructure. His trial is due to begin this fall.

Safari helicopter crash kills 7 people in Kenya, including 5 Americans
A helicopter taking tourists on a safari crashed Wednesday in a remote part of northern Kenya, killing all seven people on board — six passengers and the pilot.
Five Americans were among those killed in the crash, the U.S. State Department confirmed in a statement to CBS News. They included a Florida-based Telemundo TV station manager and a well-known Miami restaurateur.
"The U.S. Embassy is in touch with local authorities and is providing consular assistance," the spokesperson said. "We extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones on their loss."
The helicopter crashed at 9:13 a.m. while flying from the Loisaba Conservancy to the Ewaso Nyiro area in Samburu County, according to the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority, which said in a statement an investigation was underway.
David Nkoroi, the police commander for Samburu, told reporters all seven people on board had died but did not reveal their identities.
Later Wednesday, NBCUniversal said its journalist José Alberto Suárez — president and general manager of Telemundo 31, Telemundo 49 and Telemundo Fort Myers–Naples, and who worked at CBS Miami in the 1990s — was among those killed in the crash.
In a memo sent to staff obtained by CBS News, NBCUniversal leaders called Suárez "a deeply respected leader and beloved friend and colleague."
"José was an exceptional colleague and mentor to many," the memo says. "He cared deeply about his teams, the communities they served and the essential role our stations play in people's lives."
Miami restaurateur Roger Duarte was killed in the crash, a statement from his family confirmed, saying they're "devastated and heartbroken."
"The magnitude of this tragedy is impossible to comprehend, and there are no words to express the depth of our pain. We ask that you keep them all and everyone who loved them in your prayers," the statement reads. "We respectfully request privacy as our families grieve this unimaginable loss."
Ecuador's transport minister said the nation's intelligence chief, Michele Sensi-Contugi, and his wife were also killed in the crash.
"Today Michele and Stephany left us too soon. Thinking of their family, especially their children and parents," Transport Minister Roberto Luque wrote on X.
The statement from the Duarte and Valls families — Duarte's wife is Nicole Valls — also named Suárez, Sensi-Contugi and Stephany Holliham Yeaza as among those who were killed, and identified the pilot and the two other passengers.
The helicopter crashed in a rugged area in the foothills of Mount Ololokwe, a popular tourist destination in the country, local media reported. The helicopter, owned by local company Lady Lori Helicopters, was carrying guests with travel company &Beyond. Lady Lori Helicopters said in a statement the aircraft was operating a charter flight when it crashed.
Tropic Air Kenya, a local safari operator, said in a statement it dispatched two of its helicopters to aid search and rescue operations.
The aviation authority said the aircraft was a Eurocopter EC130 B4.
The Kenya Red Cross said its emergency response teams were "participating in a multiagency response effort as rescue teams work to access the crash site."
"Search and recovery efforts are ongoing, hampered by difficult terrain access and an active fire at the crash site," the organization posted on social media along with images of the wreckage.
Helicopter crashes have happened with increasing regularity in Kenya, which has a vibrant tourism industry that depends on domestic carriers to ferry visitors to distant places like Mount Ololokwe.
In February, a legislator was among six people who died after a helicopter crash in a hilly area of western Kenya.
In 2019, four Americans and a local pilot were killed in Kenya when their helicopter crashed on an island in the north of the country.

Hind Rajab Foundation targeted 86 IDF soldiers abroad, but none indicted - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
18:45:30 UTC
03:45:30 KST

Pro-Palestine legal body Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) filed yet another criminal complaint against an IDF soldier abroad, this time in India.
For at least two and a half years, the Belgian-based organization has been repeatedly filing legal complaints, requesting arrest warrants and filing with the International Criminal Court regarding IDF soldiers it accuses of war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide in Gaza.
For the most part, the basis of HRF’s accusations is footage from social media or open-source intelligence pinning specific individuals to an alleged war crime in Gaza.
In some cases, like with the most recent petition in India on Tuesday, HRF targets soldiers while they are traveling.
At other times, it targets dual-national soldiers by filing a criminal complaint in their other country of origin.
HRF targeted at least 86 individuals in 30 countries
The Jerusalem Post has reviewed every legal complaint by HRF against IDF soldiers abroad since it opened (excluding politicians, non-soldiers, and entire battalions).
To date, HRF has filed against at least 86 individuals in at least 30 countries.
HRF’s method is often referred to as lawfare – filing large quantities of complaints against individuals with the hope that some of them successfully end in legal measures being taken, as well as, of course, raising the visibility of HRF’s cause.
But how many of these complaints against the at least 86 soldiers actually resulted in concrete legal action?
According to the Post’s analysis, complaints against 11 of the 86 individuals (13%) resulted in substantive action by the country’s authorities.
Complaints result in investigations and questioning
For example, in July 2025, two IDF soldiers attending the Tomorrowland Festival in Belgium were detained and questioned by local authorities. The Belgian Federal Prosecutor did refer the dossiers to the ICC through the Justice Ministry, but no charges were made.
In Peru in June 2025, the Public Prosecutor’s Office formally opened a criminal investigation after HRF’s complaint against an individual. This has not yet led to any action.
In Brazil, a federal judge ordered the Federal Police to investigate an IDF soldier in January 2025, but he left Brazil before police could act.
The Federal Police later sought reconsideration or closure of the investigation, but took no further action.
Chilean reporting stated that the Centro Norte prosecutor’s office activated an investigation into a soldier following a complaint, but no charge was made.
Other countries followed a similar pattern: for example, soldier and comedian Guy Hochman was detained and questioned in Canada after an HRF complaint, but was released.
The Post found other cases in Greece and Romania.
Then, in Lithuania, the Prosecutor General’s Office considered HRF’s request but refused to open a pretrial investigation.
In Spain, the Central Investigative Court No. 5 rejected a complaint against a soldier in September 2025.
No foreign indictments arising from HRF complaints
As of Wednesday, despite the Post finding a number of cases where an HRF complaint produced some form of action by the country involved, no foreign indictment, prosecution, trial, or conviction of any soldier has arisen from an HRF complaint.
This distinction matters because a criminal complaint itself does not mean a country’s authorities have concluded that a crime was committed. Nor does detention, questioning, or a preliminary investigation amount to a criminal charge.
HRF’s campaign therefore appears to operate on two levels: the pursuit of potential legal action against individual soldiers, and the broader political and reputational pressure created by repeatedly bringing allegations of war crimes before national authorities around the world.
HRF’s campaign has been successful in generating visibility, pressure and occasional disruption for individual soldiers.

'He has 57 powerful nuclear weapons': Trump says he will meet North Korea's Kim Jong Un
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
18:45:05 UTC
03:45:05 KST

US President Donald Trump confirmed on Wednesday that he plans to meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his upcoming visit to Asia, telling reporters at the White House that maintaining a good relationship with Kim was important given North Korea's nuclear arsenal.
Trump then addressed his relationship with the North Korean leader, emphasizing that "the fact that I get along with him is a good thing, because he has 57 very powerful nuclear weapons."
Trump also addressed the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, claiming that the United States has "complete control" of the waterway.
Earlier on Monday, Trump said he had received a response from Kim following his attempts to reengage. The Wall Street Journal reported that he has pushed aides to arrange an in-person meeting with Kim as soon as this autumn.
North Korea's mission to the United Nations in New York did not immediately respond to Reuters request for comment on Trump's latest remarks, but they came just after Kim's powerful sister, Kim Yo Jong, said she was unaware of any recent communications between the two countries' leaders.
Kim Yo Jong also said that while the relationship between the leaders of the United States and North Korea was "truly great," Washington was still carrying out the drills with Seoul and threatening the national security of Pyongyang.
Trump held an unprecedented series of summits with Kim in 2018 and 2019, but the diplomatic efforts broke down over US demands that North Korea give up its nuclear weapons. Trump has since referred to North Korea repeatedly as a "nuclear power," although his administration has continued to call for the country's denuclearization and does not formally recognize it as a nuclear-weapon state.
Trump aims to revive diplomatic efforts
Trump has sought to revive the diplomatic efforts in his second term.
"I know Kim Jong Un very well, and he's going to be fine as long as we have a smart president," he told reporters on Wednesday during a tour of a helipad he is constructing on the White House's historic South Lawn.
"The fact that I get along with him - that's a good thing, not a bad thing. He has 57 very powerful nuclear weapons," Trump said. "They should have never allowed it. If I were president, I wouldn't have allowed it. But he's got them."
Trump's citing of a specific number of nuclear weapons held by North Korea was highly unusual.
No official estimates of North Korea's nuclear weapons
The US government does not publicly publish an official estimate of North Korea's nuclear arsenal, although a 2025 report by the Congressional Research Service cited non-governmental experts as estimating that North Korea has produced enough fissile material for up to 90 warheads but may have assembled approximately 50.
In June, the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute estimated that North Korea has "possibly assembled around 60 warheads, possesses enough fissile material to produce at least 30 more."
During Trump's first term, Kim called Trump a “mentally deranged US dotard” and threatened that he had use of a "nuclear button" on his desk.
But the two leaders turned that tension into face-to-face meetings, including a brief exchange at the demilitarized zone between the Koreas in which Trump became the first sitting US president to step into North Korean territory.

Israel, Turkey maneuver toward potential clash over influence in Syria - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
18:45:01 UTC
03:45:01 KST

Israel’s recent airstrike on Syria forms part of a larger context of tensions between Israel and Turkey over Syria. Some Israeli officials believe that there could be a future clash in Syria.
This kind of rhetoric has led to predictions in Jerusalem that there will be a war either with Syria or possibly with both Syria and Turkey. The argument is that Syria is dominated by a right-leaning Sunni Muslim government.
For Israel’s critics of Syria, the perception is that Damascus is led by “jihadists,” and these are allied with Turkey’s ruling AKP party. The AKP has roots in the Muslim Brotherhood.
Therefore, the perception in Jerusalem is that Israel potentially faces a Muslim Brotherhood axis that will replace the Iranian-led axis. This “Sunni” threat is increasingly being discussed.
Israel's evolving policy in Syria
Rhetoric is one thing. Action is another. The bombing of Syria is not entirely new. Israel carried out thousands of airstrikes before the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024.
Those strikes were aimed at preventing Iranian entrenchment in Syria. This was called the Campaign Between the Wars. It became a campaign of precision strikes.
This showed the limitations of using air power. The strikes didn’t stop Iran’s weapon smuggling to Hezbollah via Syria. All the airstrikes did was reduce the threat.
Israel didn’t entirely learn the lessons of the Campaign Between the Wars. Instead, the policy was extended after the fall of the Assad regime.
Instead of doing outreach to the new government in Damascus, Jerusalem preferred to continue attacks on Syria and to extend Israeli control on the ground into a buffer zone along the border.
Tensions grew in 2025. Israel said it would protect the Druze minority in southern Syria. This led to some Druze leaders believing they could potentially create an independent Druze state in Suwayda.
Damascus, Amman, and others oppose this initiative. However, Israel’s mission creep in Syria, from fighting Iran to attacking the new government to backing the Druze, has led to an open-ended policy that could grow to also include clashes with Turkey.
Turkey's growing role in post-Assad Syria
Why would there be clashes with Turkey? Turkey has been a major supporter of the new government in Damascus. Ankara had been backing some Syrian rebels before the fall of Assad.
However, Ankara cynically used these rebels to fight Kurdish forces. After the fall of Assad, Turkey seized the opportunity to work with Ahmed al-Shara’a, the president of Syria. Turkey’s policy was joined by Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and other countries in embracing Damascus.
This led to meetings between US President Donald Trump and Shara’a. Trump has embraced the new Syrian leadership. Turkey is a NATO ally of the US, and Qatar is a major non-NATO ally. Trump is also close with Saudi Arabia’s leadership.
The US has opposed Israel’s strikes on Syria in the past. In fact, after strikes in Damascus in the summer of 2025, the Trump administration sought to prevent further tensions. Trump wants Syria to be stable.
The administration worked toward trilateral meetings between Syria, Israel, and the US. However, the White House has also had to juggle policies in Gaza and Lebanon, where the US is working on peace deals. The US can’t be involved on all of Israel’s borders. This leaves room for tensions to grow with Turkey in Syria.
Israel’s current leadership wants to send Ankara a message that Turkey should not expand its role. Israel’s foreign ministry has often condemned Turkey’s role in northern Syria. Turkey invaded northern Syria several times since 2016.
After the fall of Assad, Turkey has shifted its role to back the new government. Israel’s main concern appears to be that Turkey may rehabilitate strategic sites, such as air bases.
The Prime Minister's Office said Tuesday that Syria nearly breached the "status quo" the two countries reached after Assad's fall because of the reported Turkish military presence in Syria.
“Israel and Syria agreed to a status quo in security matters, which Syria was on the verge of breaching by permitting Turkish troops to deploy at an airbase near Aleppo," the PMO said in a statement.
"Israel repeatedly warned Syria that such a deployment would pose a threat to Israel's security. Syria chose to ignore these warnings.”
Meanwhile, Israel’s Chief of the General Staff went to the Security Zone in Syria on Wednesday. “We see what is happening and are monitoring the changes on the Syrian front; we will not allow hostile forces to establish themselves on our borders, and we will know how to use our operational capabilities precisely where and when needed,” he said.
“We must prevent the development of terrorist threats, while also preventing the formation of a significant military threat on our borders”
Zamir added that “we are still in a multi-front war, alert and operating in all arenas, escalation can develop in any one of them, and we must remain in constant readiness for that.”
Ankara seeks to downplay potential confrontation
Turkey is currently trying to downplay the potential clash. Turkish media views the Israeli strike as being related to Israel’s upcoming elections. Turkey’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has been at the forefront of discussions about Israel.
Turkey’s pro-government Daily Sabah noted last week that “Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan’s remarks in recent days can be regarded as one of the strongest warnings Turkey has delivered to Israel to date.
Fidan warned Israel not to undermine the Gaza agreement, stating that Türkiye, Qatar and Egypt could take “radical measures” if Israel attempts to derail the agreement. His remarks offer an important indication of how Ankara intends to approach the Gaza issue in the period ahead.”
A recent article in Al-Hurra noted that Israel is watching Hakan Fidan as a potential successor to Turkey’s long-time leader Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
The challenge for Israel and Turkey in Syria is that both countries have been led by the same leadership for most of the last two decades. Israel is led by a right-leaning nationalist and religious government, and so is Turkey.
While Israel’s government is a coalition, and Turkey’s is primarily led by the AKP, the reality is that both countries have a natural tendency to see the region in Manichean terms.
Erdogan’s anti-Israel comments go back many years. The clash over the Mavi Marmara, a large ship used by Turkish activists to try to reach Gaza in 2010, is one example of how Turkey-Israel relations soured. Another reason was the 2009 war in Gaza. Ankara has also hosted Hamas leaders in the past.
Could Israel and Turkey clash in Syria?
There is now a sense that a clash in Syria is inevitable. Turkey is maneuvering with caution. It doesn’t want to fight Israel yet. Damascus is very pragmatic. It doesn’t want a clash with Israel.
However, Jerusalem's rhetoric is clear. Leading voices expect a war with Syria. Others view Turkey as the “new Iran.” This means that even though Iran is not yet defeated, and neither are Hezbollah and Hamas, Turkey could be dragged into a potential conflict.
On the ground on the Golan, the view is more tactical. As Israel’s Chief of Staff noted, the goal is to prevent threats reaching the border. This is part of the post-October 7 tactic of creating buffer zones in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria. Turkey is nowhere near the Golan yet.
However, the messaging to Ankara is similar to the messaging to Iran before the fall of the Assad regime. Israel wants to prevent foreign forces from entrenching in Syria. Syria is now seen as Israel’s “near abroad” and basically an area where Israel wants a zone of influence or even control.
This will likely also mean Jerusalem demanding freedom of action in Syria’s skies. It is unclear when Turkey will seek to extend its own zone of influence. However, if Ankara asserts its right to do so, a clash could follow.
Israel de-conflicted with Russia in Syria in the Assad era. In fact, Israeli officials went to Russia in 2015 when Russia intervened in Syria to back Assad during the civil war. Not everything worked in Syria with Russia.
Syrian air defense shot down a Russian military aircraft while trying to strike at Israeli planes in 2018. This led to a crisis. Russia and Turkey also had several small crises in Syria.
US could play a role in reducing tensions
It remains to be seen how Turkey and Israel will manage their policy in Syria. The US could help broker a deal and reduce tensions. However, the US is focused also on Iran, Gaza, Lebanon and many other issues in the region.
US Ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack, who is also envoy to Syria and Iraq, noted on X/ Twitter on August 18 “We are deeply concerned that the confirmed Israeli airstrikes on Abu al-Duhur Airbase constitute an unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability. The Al-Sharra government has neither adopted a predatory posture nor maintained proxy forces. It has, in fact, repeatedly indicated a preference for de-escalation with Israel. The United States has in the past, and will continue in the future, to host discussions to encourage diplomatic cadence over kinetic frustration for both nations.”
He added that “the United States continues to believe that restraint and engagement offer the more constructive course. We encourage all parties to prioritize logical discourse over further military incidents.”

WATCH: Anti-Israel MMA fighter gets knocked out after challenging Zionists in Tel Aviv to fight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
18:44:59 UTC
03:44:59 KST

Ten days after publishing a video to his Instagram account with the challenge “come fight me Zios” in “Tel Aviv, occupied Palestine,” pro-Palestinian influencer Ido Amiaz, also known as “the Salukie,” found himself knocked down three times in a boxing match that ended in a technical knockout after around 40 seconds.
Amiaz, an Israeli-born anti-Zionist influencer who has built a following through videos documenting his activism in the West Bank and now describes himself as a journalist in Palestine, was fighting Israeli mixed martial artist Shimon Smotritsky.
Smotritsky previously posted a video accepting the fight on his Instagram account on August 9, one day after the anti-Zionist influencer issued the challenge.
In later comments to The Jerusalem Post, Smotritsky said that the minute he saw Amiaz's challenge, he knew "that's my opportunity to shut him up."
"This guy is always spreading lies about Israel, about IDF soldiers, about all the heroes that are protecting us. And he's saying things that are against my values, against the truth. So, I knew I needed to make him quiet and teach him a lesson."
In Amiaz's initial video in which he issued the challenge, he said that he had had the idea to fight for some time because he was getting daily threats to fight him in Israel.
Amiaz's challenge to Zionists: 'Meet here in Tel Aviv. I’m waiting'
“So, this is an open invitation. Write me a DM, and we meet here in Tel Aviv. I’m waiting. B***h,” he said.
In his response video, Smotritsky accepted the challenge, adding, “now let’s see if you will actually stand up behind your words and fight an Israeli, or you will act like a typical Palestinian troll: you'll talk s**t about Israelis and then when we respond, you will cry on social media and say that we are the bullies and the aggressors like you always do.”
Amiaz’s response followed the same day, mocking Smotritsky and speaking Hebrew in a Russian accent, saying, “I hear your accent, my dear. Definitely very indigenous to the region!”
He went on to complain that he had been planning on fighting “normal Zios,” rather than a professional fighter, but that “as per usual, you people don’t like to play fair,” noting that he had received direct messages from a number of Israeli MMA fighters accepting the challenge.
He added, though, that he would keep his word, despite a prediction that the fighters would “tear me a new a*****e.”
Videos published to his account over the following days addressed the fight in various ways. One showed him as he trained to box, another dismissed accusations that he would back out of the fight, and another jokingly asked his audience if they would donate for facial reconstruction surgery.
In another, after an Israeli man asked him on a train ride if he’s been training and if he had a message he was trying to send, Amiaz complained “I can’t even take the choo-choo these days without the Chosen Crew convening an impromptu extemporaneous pre-fight conference.”
Amiaz brought Amir Hetsroni, an Israeli anti-Zionist academic, with him to the fight.
Hetsroni is widely known in Israel as a provocateur, a description he has denied despite a public record of inflammatory statements and high-profile controversies.
After the third and final time Smotritsky knocked Amiaz down in the boxing match between the two, the referee stopped the fight, declaring it a technical knockout.
Speaking shortly thereafter, Smotritsky expressed his surprise that Amiaz showed up to the fight, adding that doing so had earned his respect.
“Everyone curses me and threatens me, saying they’re going to kill me. Saluki challenged a Zionist fighter, and he showed up. For that alone, I respect you. I don’t agree with your views at all, and I think you’re a troll, but at the end of the day, you wanted this, and you got it,” Smotritsky said.
“Next time someone wants to represent Palestinians and fight against a Zionist, I want a bigger challenge. So, Belal Muhammad, Adam Salah, any one of you p*****s that talks s**t about my country, come get it.”
In his later comments to the Post, Smotritsky said that his fight with Amiaz wasn't a challenge for him.
"It was easy work for me," he said. "I don't even consider it as a fight. And I hope I beat some Zionism into this guy."
Lital Davidov contributed to this article.

Zambia opposition leader to challenge Hichilema election victory in court
Mundubile claims his campaign documented ‘serious irregularities’ around the vote that handed President Hakainde Hichilema a second term.
Zambian opposition leader Brian Mundubile says he will challenge the country’s presidential election result in court, alleging voting fraud in the contest that handed President Hakainde Hichilema a second term in office.
“Our campaign has documented serious irregularities, inconsistencies and circumstances surrounding the conduct, counting, transmission and declaration of results,” Mundubile said in a statement on Wednesday.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Zambia’s president extends election lead as contested vote count continues
- list 2 of 4Zambia’s President Hakainde Hichilema wins second term
- list 3 of 4Hichilema wins second term as president of copper-rich Zambia
- list 4 of 4Hichilema re-elected as Zambia president amid opposition concerns over vote
While last week’s vote was largely peaceful, the opposition said intimidation and restrictions marred its campaign, concerns echoed by international election observers.
The election commission declared Hichilema the winner with about 60 percent of votes in the early morning Tuesday, compared with 38 percent for Mundubile.
After a relatively quiet run-up to the August 13 election in the nation of 22 million people, tensions escalated rapidly after the polls closed.
The authorities arrested 11 people, including leading opposition figures in a raid that involved an exchange of gunfire while Mundubile was present.
The electoral commission also suspended vote-counting for hours due to reports of violence against polling staff and ballot paper theft.
United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said on Wednesday that he was concerned over the arrest of the opposition officials.
All arrests “must be fully consistent with international human rights standards, as well as Zambian domestic law”, Turk said in a statement.
Hichilema entered the race as the clear favourite after steering Zambia through a major economic turnaround and restructuring its debt.
But his first term was also marked by concerns over Zambia’s political space, with opposition parties and civil society groups accusing his government of curbing dissent.
The incumbent leader’s second term will be shaped by demands for stronger accountability, national unity and broader benefits from economic growth.
Hichilema is due to be sworn in within seven days of the commission publishing the official results, due by August 24, but the planned challenge by the opposition could delay the process.

Liberia says it's taking in 1,200 third-country US deportees
August 19, 2026
Liberia has agreed to accept up to 1,200 third-country deportees from the United States in the next 12 months, the government said this week.
It said that the first group of 20 were expected to arrive on Thursday.
Donald Trump's administration has recently struck several deals with African countries to take in people it cannot legally send back to their home countries — typically because of US court orders ruling that doing so would put them in danger.
What did Liberia say about the agreement?
"Liberia intends to accept up to 1,200 persons to be transferred from the United States of America within a year," the Liberian government said in a statement published on Tuesday.
It said that the people would be received "as guests" and that they would be "free to depart the country when they so desire" or to apply for asylum.
The government's statement said the deportees "will include citizens or nationals of African and Western Hemisphere countries who are medically authorized to travel."
It said that the deal did not involve a quid pro quo with the US and that it was not demanding and had not received any direct compensation.
However, it also said that it would receive "support to help manage the program and strengthen its migration system more broadly," without elaborating.
The statement also referenced Liberia's 19th century history as a refuge for freed slaves from the US, and its "long history of accepting people seeking refuge from political and other crises."
Why is the US looking for support of this kind from African countries?
The announcement follows around a year after Liberian President Joseph Boakai visited the White House among a group of African leaders and held talks with Trump.
Seeking a way to deport would-be migrants that it cannot send back to their countries of origin — very often because of US courts ruling that doing so would put them at risk of torture or other abuses — the Trump administration has been seeking agreements with third countries willing to take some of the people.
The US government has defended such agreements as lawful, although some rights groups and advocates have said the details are often opaque and that many of the deportees are ultimately repatriated.
Beyond Monrovia's description, no information was immediately available on where exactly the deportees hailed from.
Other African countries including the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Central African Republic, Equatorian Guinea, Cameroon, Ghana and Sierra Leone have reached similar accords with the US.
The EU is currently looking into somewhat comparable plans that would allow member states to send rejected asylum seekers to so-called "return hubs" in third countries as part of bilateral or multilateral agreements, provided various conditions were met.

Uber orders among accidental personal charges repaid by public servants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
18:38:54 UTC
03:38:54 KST

Public servants repay hundreds of thousands of dollars in personal charges
In short:
Public servants have incurred hundreds of thousands of dollars in inadvertent personal charges on work-issued credit cards, including Uber Eats orders.
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher has expressed confidence in the processes in place to manage credit card usage across departments and agencies.
What's next?
All accidental personal expenses must be paid back, and the vast majority already have been repaid.
Public servants have had to hand back hundreds of thousands of dollars in inadvertent personal charges, including food delivery orders, incurred on taxpayer-funded credit cards.
New figures provided to the Senate detail thousands of transactions in the past financial year where workers across multiple departments breached credit card rules.
At the Home Affairs Department, employees were required to repay 477 purchases made between July last year and March this year worth $28,400.
The accidental personal purchases included 149 transactions valued at about $5,500 that were related to Uber or Uber Eats.
A spokesperson for the department said all private expenditure must be repaid and it had processes to "support the appropriate use" of credit cards.
"Accidental personal expenditure can arise across a range of categories, for example purchases from restaurants, fast food and convenience stores as well as taxis," they said.
Public servants at the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) were also required to repay roughly $151,000 in personal charges last financial year.
The largest of the 2,029 inadvertent transactions was worth more than $3,000 and was repaid in full.
A DFAT spokesperson noted its policies banned private expenditure on corporate credit cards and said any personal transaction charged in error must be repaid.
At the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet, workers had to reimburse 81 inadvertent purchases worth about $2,400, with most of them relating to Uber.
In a statement, Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said she had confidence in the processes in place to manage credit card usage in departments and agencies.
"The information presented shows that the system is working — in that inappropriate use is identified and paid back," she said.
"Agencies and secretaries are required to manage this appropriately at departmental level."
However, Deputy Opposition Leader Jane Hume said thousands of inappropriate transactions across government raised legitimate questions about whether existing controls were sufficiently effective.
"While it is encouraging that these purchases are identified and the vast majority repaid, the scale is concerning," she said.
AFP among agencies and departments misusing credit cards
The Australian Federal Police (AFP) also recorded 987 erroneous personal transactions on corporate credit cards last financial year valued at more than $42,000.
"Where inadvertent personal expenses are incurred, they must be repaid within one working day of the member becoming aware of the accidental use," an AFP spokesperson said.
Employees at the Health Department accumulated about $5,370 in accidental private purchases in the 2025-26 financial year.
A spokesperson for the department said it undertook compliance reviews and that cardholders cannot withdraw cash from their credit cards.
The Department of Employment and Workplace Relations also recorded $8,688 in inadvertent personal purchases, all of which were repaid.
At the Department of Social Services, $2,250 in accidental personal purchases on work credit cards were paid back.
Both the employment and social services departments noted personal purchases were banned on work-issued credit cards.
The Department of Defence meanwhile recorded 3,276 purchases valued at about $240,000 that it described as "contrary to Defence policy".
The department has confirmed at least $213,672 of it has been paid back.
"Defence maintains a strong compliance and control framework to ensure inadvertent personal purchases are identified and addressed," a spokesperson said.

At least 100 killed in gold mine collapse in Central African Republic

Unknown Publisher

18:36:15 UTC
03:36:15 KST

ALBAWABA- At least 100 people were killed when an artisanal gold mine collapsed in the western Central African Republic on Tuesday, with local sources reporting that as many as 107 bodies had been recovered. The death toll could rise as rescue teams continue searching for miners believed to be trapped beneath the debris.
The collapse occurred at a gold-mining site in Zamboye, in Nana-Mambéré prefecture near the border with Cameroon. The site is about 50 kilometers from the Central African town of Baboua and lies near Garoua-Boulaï on the Cameroonian side of the border.
Witnesses and local officials said the ground suddenly gave way, burying miners working in open pits and underground tunnels. A miner, Cédric Mbango, described the incident as catastrophic, saying the ground collapsed completely and buried workers.
Residents and volunteers began digging through the debris with limited equipment in an effort to recover victims and search for survivors. More than 100 bodies had reportedly been recovered by Wednesday, while several injured miners were taken to hospitals in Baboua and Bouar. Some miners remained missing or trapped, although rescuers said the chances of finding additional survivors were diminishing.
The collapse has highlighted the dangerous conditions in the Central African Republic’s artisanal mining sector, where miners frequently work in deep pits and makeshift underground tunnels with little or no safety equipment or engineering oversight. Local officials said the Zamboye site was operating without adequate safety standards, raising questions about regulation and responsibility for the disaster.
The Baboua prosecutor’s office has opened an investigation into the collapse, including the condition of the underground tunnels, the circumstances surrounding the accident and the potential responsibility of those operating the site. Authorities are also working to identify the victims and determine the final death toll.
Government spokesman Evariste Ngamana expressed condolences to the victims’ families and said authorities were working to provide assistance. Local officials have appealed for additional support for the rescue and recovery operation.
Artisanal gold mining is widespread across the Central African Republic, where poverty, limited employment opportunities and weak state presence have pushed thousands of people into informal mining. The sector provides an important source of income for communities but is frequently associated with hazardous working conditions, unregulated excavation and inadequate safety measures.

Air Forces Southern Focuses on Intel Sharing for Major SOUTHCOM Exercise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
18:30:43 UTC
03:30:43 KST

A major U.S. Southern Command exercise this month brought representatives from 10 Latin American countries to Davis-Monthan Air Force Base, Ariz., for the air component of the event, with a focus on intelligence sharing for coordinating air operations.
PANAMAX, which ran Aug. 3-14, is one of Southern Command’s biggest annual multinational exercises, and Air Forces Southern regularly hosts participants at Davis-Monthan to contribute to running an air operations center like AFSOUTH’s 612th AOC.
This year’s edition had a few new wrinkles. For one, it was the first time Ecuador sent an air intelligence officer, as the violence-stricken nation receives direct U.S. military support.
“Collaborating in a combined air component environment allows us to synchronize our procedures and learn from each other’s expertise,” Lt. Col. Andres Acosta, operations, intelligence, and analysis officer for the Ecuadorian Air Force, said in a release. “This training ensures that if we are called upon to respond to a real-world contingency, we can operate seamlessly as one united team to preserve regional stability.”
Including the new intelligence officer deepened key goals for the exercise, an Air Forces Southern spokesperson said in an email response to Air & Space Forces Magazine.
“Having Ecuadorian intelligence embedded in the 612th AOC allowed the combined air component to process simulated scenario data in real-time, building the exact trust and joint operational habits required for a rapid coalition response,” the spokesperson wrote.
The bilateral training focused “heavily” on standardizing communication protocols and “operationalizing shared air doctrine,” the spokesperson wrote.
“While we cannot discuss specific communication architecture, the exercise prioritized integrating intelligence-sharing frameworks to establish a common, rapid threat-assessment process across participating Western Hemisphere nations,” the spokesperson added.
SOUTHCOM did not respond to a request for comment.
This year’s exercise also unfolded against the backdrop of a larger shift in U.S. military posture across the Western Hemisphere and a growing emphasis on the counternarcotics mission, including the formation of the Americas Counter Cartels Coalition, a 19-nation partnership across the region.
“Over time the exercise has expanded to include counternarcotics, cybersecurity, as well as medical missions to nearby communities,” Henry Ziemer, a fellow with the Americas Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “This year the exercise has taken on added significance as an opportunity for the United States to reiterate its commitment to its Western Hemisphere partners following the launch of the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition.”
On Aug. 3, SOUTHCOM head Marine Corps Gen. Francis L. Donovan announced that the temporary Operation Southern Spear would transition to Joint Task Force-Western Hemisphere, a more permanent presence to counter cartels, narco-terrorists, and traffickers in the command’s area of operations. The task force will be the “action arm for confronting threats across the hemisphere,” Donovan said.
The new task force synchronizes wider military operations with partner nations in the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition as well as rapid response to various crises and humanitarian needs. That’s in addition to the long-running Joint Interagency Task Force-South, which is meant to find, fix, and target illicit drug trafficking and other cross-border criminal networks in both maritime and air domains.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth traveled to Panama last week to participate in PANAMAX and to address a conference for the ACCC
“The new motto of the ACCC is we do bad things to bad people,” Hegseth said. “That’s the mentality I want to have inside this room. Now we’re good people that do good things. But ultimately, we’re dealing with bad people that have done a lot of bad things to a lot of good people for a very long time.”
While air strikes on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and the eastern Pacific were the initial public displays of Southern Spear, a shift to more internal operations with the cooperation of partner and ally nations looks forthcoming.
Ecuador was the first nation to receive such direct support under the new ACCC framework within its own borders.
Ecuador’s Role
Under previous Ecuadorian presidential administrations, military cooperation with the United States was virtually nonexistent, Ziemer said.
But it has “surged” as Ecuador confronts criminal violence and insecurity.
“Today, Ecuador is engaging in unprecedented levels of cooperation with SOUTHCOM and has become one of the foremost advocates for Washington’s more hardline security strategy in the Americas,” Ziemer said.
On March 3, the United States began direct military support to Ecuador to combat ongoing violence triggered in 2024 when gang leader Adolfo “Fito” Macías escaped prison, and cartel members attacked a live TV broadcast in Guayaquil and set off car bombs in various locations.
Those actions have escalated over the past two years in a series of incidents that have included attacks by local cartels Los Choneros and Los Lobos.
Ecuador has been part of PANAMAX for the past 15 years, primarily in maritime and land components. This was the first time the exercise has had a field component since 2012, which started in 2003 with Chile, Panama, and the United States.
Ecuador’s geographic position, an Andean nation between Colombia and Peru, the two top cocaine producers in the world, makes it a crucial ally for intelligence gathering against cartel operations and countering other types of trafficking, retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Norman Seip told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
“It’s critical when you take a look at what goes on in Colombia from drug trafficking. We’ll just talk drug trafficking. What goes on in Colombia? What goes on in Panama? What goes on in Central America? And look at Ecuador. It sits smack in the middle of all that, as well as Peru,” Seip said. “Their participation, their involvement, their collaboration, their coordination is critical, at least from the standpoint of the counter-narcotics fight that we’re in, to have them on board.”
The former 12th Air Force commander, who now serves as president of the nonprofit think tank American Security Project, said that having intelligence inside partner and allied nations in the counter-cartel fight is vital.
Ziemer added: “The presence of the first-ever contingent of Ecuadorian Air Force intelligence personnel at PANAMAX indicates the growing strength of the U.S.-Ecuador security partnership. Their presence will likely strengthen interoperability between Ecuador and the United States along with regional partners.”
The Air Focus
As exercises like PANAMAX expand and the new joint task force revs up, work for the 12th Air Force and other air components is likely to grow. Building intelligence capacity and sharing with the regional partners will be key to managing this.
The primary assistance the 12th Air Force can provide to Ecuador and other allies, both Seip and Ziemer told Air & Space Forces Magazine, is intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance assets.
“Transitioning key regional partners from information consumers to active, mutual contributors exponentially enhances regional air domain awareness,” the AFSOUTH spokesperson wrote. “Standardizing and expediting intelligence-sharing frameworks enables more immediate, coordinated responses to illicit aerial trafficking, ultimately creating a more robust, collective air shield against transnational criminal organizations.
The 66th Annual Conference of American Air Chiefs, held in the Dominican Republic in June, focused on airspace control, a historic strategic shift and a new “third line of effort,” according to a June release from Air Forces Southern.
The Fuerza Aérea Ecuatoriana, the Ecuadorian Air Force, operates the Embraer A-29 Super Tucano, a turboprop light attack aircraft, and the Airbus C-295, De Havilland DHC-6 Twin Otter. As part of the partner capacity-building work in the region, the 12th Air Force also coordinated a $13 million modernization program for FAE surveillance radars for domestic air domain awareness, the spokesperson wrote.

Keen to plant native flowers in your garden? We asked an expert for tips
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Expert tips on how to help Australia's native plants thrive in your garden
This National Science Week, we're celebrating all things native wildflowers.
But while they look gorgeous out in the wild, they can be a little tricky to grow in your garden — particularly if you're used to nurturing non-natives.
To try and help, we've compiled the best tips and tricks to try and make your wildflowers thrive.
The most important rule, according to King's Park and Botanic Garden plant breeder Digby Growns, is to not expect all natives to be low maintenance or require the same things.
"It's horses for courses," he says.
"Some plants are more adaptable than others so try and start off with ones that are a bit tougher."
Can I grow any native plant?
Australia is a big place, and there are lots of different climates and environments, from deserts to rainforests, for plants to grow.
Mr Growns says that understanding where your plant is from and their needs helps avoid many beginner problems.
"If you're trying to grow West Australian plants, for instance, they generally need a really, really well-drained, almost sand-type soil," he says.
"So the number-one rule is to understand where your plants are from."
Some species are versatile, growing across many regions.
Other plants exist in smaller areas and may struggle when moved to new climates.
But, there are ways to get beautiful plants from around the country, you just need to know what you're looking for.
Kangaroo paws, for example, are native to southern Western Australia, but there are now cultivars bred to suit different conditions.
The original species — Anigozanthos flavidus — does best in its local area but hybrid cultivars can be grown widely and have more variation in flower colour, height, flower size, disease resilience and climate and soil adaptability.
How much upkeep is needed?
The amount of time you can spend gardening is a major factor when picking plants to grow.
Some Australian native plants, such as basket grass (Lomandra) and bottlebrushes (Callistemon) need little maintenance. While others, like native orchids for example, can require much more effort and know-how.
Take the time to choose the right plant, and you can save yourself time and money, according to Mr Growns.
He said that many botanical gardens, like King's Park have varieties of native species that are "pretty much bulletproof" and recommended as starter plants for gardeners who "struggle with a brown thumb".
For instance, Perth-based gardeners might like to try Ashby's banksia (Banksia ashbyi subsp. boreoscaia), grey cottonhead (Conostylis candicans) and the heart-leaf flame pea (Chorizema cordatum).
Do you need fire for native seeds?
Some of Australia's plants are activated only after a wildfire has gone through the area.
This is the case with some species of the flannel flower, one of the natives in this year's National Science Week poll to find the most amazing wildflower.
The flower blooms prolifically in the wild after bushfires, but to grow the plant yourself you don't need to light anything on fire.
"The seeds are recalcitrant and they require smoke water or aerosol smoke treatment to germinate," Mr Growns says.
"Kangaroo paws from seed need the same."
Importantly, the seeds you buy from a nursery will be pre-smoked, so they should grow without fire required.
You also don't necessarily need to grow natives from seed.
"There's quite a number of plants you can grow from cuttings," Mr Growns said.
"Some of the Calytrix [star flowers] you can, and small myrtaceous plants like melaleucas."
How often should I water natives?
While it will depend on the specific plant, there are a few tips and tricks that will work with a large number of natives.
Plant during mild weather months and, even if your chosen species is drought tolerant, it's recommended to water regularly until established.
This is because nursery plants are used to more water, so tapering them off stops the plants drying out.
Speaking of watering, it's a myth that Australian native plants don't need watering.
If you want a no-water native garden, choose plants that come from a similar rainfall and weather pattern as where you live.
In a garden with a collection of Australian native plants with differing water requirements, supplementary irrigation is essential.
Use drip irrigation and do two to three deep soakings throughout the warmer weather.
Pruning is also a good idea for many natives.
For timing, the best rule of thumb is to trim immediately after a plant finishes flowering unless you want the seeds.
Remove up to a third of the growth, but don't cut down to bare wood where there's no leaves as this can result in a bare patch where nothing regrows.
Do I need different fertiliser?
If a plant is local to your area and soil type, the chances are it won't need a lot of interference or supplementary feeding.
But if you are looking at plants from across Australia keep in mind that they grow in different soils, climates and habitats so they all have different needs.
Some plants in the Proteaceae family, like banksias, grevilleas and hakeas, are quite sensitive to the amount of phosphorous found in general fertilisers.
These plants are very good at taking up existing phosphorous in the environment so a general fertiliser can be toxic.
There are plenty of low-phosphorous fertilisers that can be used instead for this group of plants and, if you want to keep things simple, you can use that same fertiliser on any other native plants in your garden too.
Potted plants are a different story, growing in isolation to the natural soil.
Top-dress containers of native plants every six months, using a slow-release fertiliser formulated for Australian plants.
Mr Growns says that no matter the native, your local nursery should be able to help get you started.
"Some nurseries like the big chain stores don't always have people that are fully across that [information on natives].
"But my recommendation is always go to a specialist nursery where you can."

Peter Garrett on the one thing more valuable than success
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Peter Garrett on protest music, hope and Midnight Oil's legacy
Midnight Oil never made noise for the sake of it.
Politically driven and socially conscious, the legendary Australian rock band always made music with meaning, reflecting what they saw to be the greatest global and local injustices.
Frontman Peter Garrett's first exposure to protest music came early.
In his episode of ABC TV's Take 5 with Zan Rowe, he recalls hearing African American spiritual turned civil rights anthem Tell It on the Mountain by American folk trio Peter, Paul and Mary as a child.
"When these first protest records started coming out, my mum went out and bought them and started playing them endlessly," he says. "So, I could hear this from my bedroom, and then I got to know it and understand it."
The young Garrett was unaware it was a protest song. As with so much great art, his understanding of the song and its importance grew over the years.
"When I listened to it again, I was really transported not only to the memory of listening as a kid, but also what that song then became for people," he says.
"I had an awareness of now. It gave the song extra weight for me."
The making of a frontman
It wasn't long before a young Peter Garrett was putting his own voice out there.
"I started in choirs, and I really loved it," he says. "I was one of the only boys in the church choir up on the North Shore in Sydney."
Upon starting university in Canberra, Garrett leapt at the chance to take the lead role in one of the rock bands on campus.
"I'm not shy," he says. "I'm lucky. I don't have stage fright or anything like that. So, I didn't have to be urged. I was ready to go.
"It was a band called Devil's Breakfast. Probably the worst name. That's what we sounded like. We changed our name, thankfully, to Rock Island Line."
That band was short-lived, but Garrett had the bug. After leaving Canberra, he wasted no time in joining up with a new set of musicians.
"Eventually I came up to Sydney and fell in with this other bunch of young miscreants. Rob Hirst, Jim Moginie, and later Martin Rotsey, and, yeah, the rest was history," he says.
The outfit, Midnight Oil, blew up Australia's booming pub rock scene in the late 1970s thanks to songs that were as intense, urgent and energetic as their breathless live shows. In the 80s and 90s, they became a global force, troubling charts in the UK, US, Canada and Europe.
Hindsight may be 20/20, but Garrett swears he felt the magic from the outset.
"When I first came in to meet them, Rob started playing and so did Jim. They were 17 or 18, and I just looked at them, and I went, 'Wow,'" he says.
"Something in me just knew that this was very special. I never knew how far it would go."
While Garrett has often seemed the face and figurehead of Midnight Oil, powerhouse drummer Rob Hirst, who died of cancer earlier this year, was another force behind many of their most enduring songs.
"Rob and I competed with one another sometimes," Garrett says. "It's like having a frontman on the drums, who's also a great singer and a songwriter," he says.
"Always with respect. Pushing to try and always make it as good as we could."
Protest music's continued relevance
Those drawn to Midnight Oil's music and message often lament the lack of protest music making waves today.
But music with a message is still out there. For Garrett, the missives of Filipino and Murrawarri artist Dobby ring loudly.
He chooses the song Dirrpi Yuin Patjulinya for his Take 5, a highlight from Dobby's ARIA-winning 2024 concept album Warrangu: River Story, which outlines the cultural importance of the Bogan, Culgoa and Barwon Rivers, and the over-irrigation and water theft that plague them.
"I share the deep call from the heart that he has about the Murray-Darling, about what we've done to our river systems," Garrett says.
"I still don't think that we've gotten to the point with leaders, with governments, where we deeply understand how important the natural world is to us and what we're doing to it. He absolutely sums it up here. It is epic."
Any perceived dearth of protest music shouldn't be too surprising. In a precarious career environment for creatives, there are risks to sticking one's neck out. What's more, writing effective protest songs is difficult.
"Part of the challenge … is to try and have that work in a song where people don't run away from it whilst at the same time not being too self-conscious about it," Garrett says.
"[Dobby] has done it in a way which is very powerful and without reservation. It's epic in a way, and it's going right to the heart of where things are at now in country."
It's not just a young man's game.
At 76, Bruce Springsteen also knows how to make protest music that connects.
Garrett considers the live version of the Edwin Starr classic War, recorded in Minneapolis around the time of this year's ICE raids, particularly electric.
"Tonight, we ask all of you to join with us in choosing hope over fear, democracy over authoritarianism," Springsteen rages in his intro.
"The rule of law over lawlessness, ethics over unbridled corruption, resistance over complacency, unity over division, and peace over war."
For Garrett, this call is a clear example of protest music's impact.
"The way he introduces this song, and the way that they play it, says everything to me about what we all need to do in this era that we live in," Garrett says.
"The fact that he can get up and say, in a highly polarised country, this is what the times demand, he's really risen to the moment.
"It sounds as strong and as fresh and as needed as it was when he first played it, and when it was first written. Powerful. Necessary."
What drives us
Protest music is often born from rage and frustration. But the strongest examples aren't defeatist: they are driven by hope.
"Hope is realising there can be a better future through action," Garrett says. "Hope is the antidote to apathy and disinterest and cynicism.
"So, hope becomes the most important and precious commodity that we have, but not hope which is born of wishful thinking, hope that's born of an understanding that it is people who change the world. It's people acting that make the difference."
And Garrett considers hope for the future a more appealing prospect than nostalgia. Despite spending most of his 73 years as a rock star or federal politician, Garrett isn't one to dwell.
"I don't look back," he says. "It's great to yarn about it, but I don't spend much time meditating on the past.
"At my stage of the game, my most precious resource by far, apart from love and family and connection, is time. There's nothing that's more important to me now than that."
Even when performing on the stage of Sydney's Hordern Pavilion at this year's APRA Awards in tribute to Hirst, Garrett knew he had to get the job done, lest the gravity of the situation overwhelm him.
"The legacy of the band, in terms of my experience of it, it takes up so much space in how I think and feel," he says.
"If you start to get too introspective about it, or if you're always looking in the rear-vision mirror, or even assessing what it is, you're buggered."
Garrett's performance that night was not born from protest, but from celebration. But the approach remains the same no matter the task at hand.
"You've just got to be in the moment," he says.
"It's not easy to do, but it is the key. Hang in the moment, make the moment work as best as you can, and then out the door."

Tony reaches behind the bravado to a different Anthony Bourdain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Tony's baptism by fire — and oil, salt and acid — is a winner
In his book Kitchen Confidential, Anthony Bourdain wrote these words: "I was — to be frank — a spoiled, miserable, narcissistic, self-destructive and thoughtless young lout, and badly in need of a good ass-kicking."
Harsh, humbling words that somehow endear you to their subject, despite the warning label.
These words mark the beginning of what its subject would call a bildungsroman: how "Tony" became the great chef and writer Anthony Bourdain.
Tony, directed by Matt Johnson (Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie, BlackBerry) and starring Dominic Sessa (The Holdovers), is incredibly confident in its subject matter and visual language, and so convincing in its central thesis, which boils down to something like: "a good ass-kicking builds character", that it hardly needs the pretence.
Tony has an immediate look and feel to it that evokes a bygone time without being overly rose-tinted, thanks to cinematography by Michael Bauman and lighting by Chris Hill.
It's the 1970s, and we are about to see Anthony Bourdain's baptism by fire in his first-ever kitchen job in Provincetown, Cape Cod.
The food looks spectacular, the water is glistening, and the sky is as blue as can be, but this coming-of-age tale is not without its dark clouds and shadows.
A film based on a true story is not easy to nail, and biopics, in particular, often crumble under the weight of reverence for their subject.
So, it's refreshing that Tony does not shy away from showing the darker sides of the young Bourdain.
Set during a short period of his life, when the 19-year-old's pursuit of a girl led to both gruelling hardship and untold opportunity, we see him try, and spectacularly fail, to achieve his dreams of being a writer.
His wins are few, his mess-ups are innumerable, and his sardonic wit is less "rockstar TV host" and more "annoying brat".
He corrects people's grammar, insists on using academic words in regular settings, and is so cocksure in his approach to women that he fails to notice (or wilfully ignores) when he's not wanted.
The success of the flick hinges entirely on depicting Bourdain as a fallible, flawed character, without going so far as to lose audience empathy.
Good thing, then, that Dominic Sessa is more than up to the task. He may not be the spitting image of Bourdain, but his naturally lanky limbs and dark curls aid a portrayal that performs best when the actor says little to nothing at all.
Sessa embodies that "thoughtless young lout" effortlessly, with a natural magnetism that makes him easy to watch and an old-school aura that suits the 1970s well.
Though Anthony would later be known for his wordcraft, this young cad is not yet the Bourdain we know. Instead, Tony repeatedly finds himself in hot water after using his mastery of language to lie, cheat, and steal his way through life.
You won't love most of the choices he makes, but you'll still root for him, and audiences will do so regardless of how well they know the actual Bourdain.
That's the other tough thing about biopics: when it depicts a person that is so fresh in our collective memory (Bourdain became world famous in the 2000s, and died in 2018), someone who had fans by the thousands and more than a few folks who had formed parasocial relationships with him (can any writer/foodie say they hadn't?), it needs to convince everyone to get on board with one director's idea of its subject. Johnson's take is nicely balanced between love for its star and wisdom about the often dark subject matter.
Of course, artistic licence is taken with Bourdain's story here, but in choosing to show only one summer of his entire life, Johnson both limits himself creatively and gives himself room for interpretation.
It's a smart move: even Bourdain himself would likely have trouble recalling that period of his life with intense accuracy; therefore, Johnson can build his base from Kitchen Confidential and experiment on top of it.
The excellent supporting cast features Emilia Jones as Nancy, the woman who would later be Bourdain's first wife; Leo Woodall as loose-cannon line cook Sal; and Stavros Halkias as comic relief. But it's Antonio Banderas as the head chef of the Flagship restaurant who truly shines.
World-weary but never bereft of hope or passion, Banderas's "Chef" is exactly the kind of mentor that Tony needs: a quiet, self-assured man who will let him sleep on the hammock rent-free, but will wake him up with a cold bucket of seawater every morning before showing him how to make sauce from scratch. He'll make you want to run away from your ordinary job and dive into the culinary arts as soon as possible.
Though Tony follows a somewhat predictable narrative structure, it has more than enough going for it to make the cinema trip worth it: specifically, Sessa's memorable central performance, and what it says about endurance in the face of rejection, as well as following your passions to find where you belong.
Both Bourdain diehards and newcomers should walk away from this film feeling satiated.
Tony is in cinemas now.

Over the course of a single day, NATO surveillance aircraft conducted missions in two key areas — over the Black Sea and near Belarus.
This was reported by the analytical channel Coffe Report.
A U.S. ARTEMIS II reconnaissance aircraft was spotted over the Black Sea, while a NATO AWACS aircraft operated over the Baltic states and Central Europe. Another E-3 AWACS and an aerial tanker were also airborne.
The flights were likely intended to gather intelligence on Russian forces and their activities in the Baltic and Black Sea regions.
According to monitoring sources, ARTEMIS II flew over the central Black Sea, south of Crimea. The Bombardier Challenger 650, registered as N159L, is operated by the U.S. Army for reconnaissance missions and intelligence gathering.
Meanwhile, a NATO AWACS aircraft, registration number LX-N90445, operated over the Baltic states and Central Europe. The aircraft is designed for long-range radar surveillance, detecting airborne targets and coordinating air operations.
Thus, the allies likely gathered intelligence on Russian military activity in different areas at the same time. In particular, ARTEMIS II monitored the area near Crimea, while the AWACS aircraft operated over the Baltic region and Central Europe.

Türkiye says Greece’s renewable energy framework has no legal effect on its Aegean position
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
18:26:10 UTC
03:26:10 KST

Seyit Kurt
19 August 2026•Update: 19 August 2026
Greece’s newly announced renewable energy spatial framework covering the Aegean Sea will have no legal consequences for Türkiye regarding the interconnected disputes between the two countries, the Turkish Foreign Ministry said Wednesday.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Oncu Keceli said the framework, like similar Greek initiatives, would have no legal effect on Türkiye, including with regard to geographical formations whose sovereignty was not transferred to Greece under international treaties.
“As we have emphasized on various occasions in the past, this and similar initiatives will not affect Türkiye’s legal position regarding Aegean issues,” Keceli said in a statement on US social media platform X.
Keceli stressed that unilateral actions should be avoided in enclosed or semi-enclosed seas such as the Aegean and Mediterranean, noting that international maritime law encourages cooperation among coastal states in such waters.
He reiterated that Türkiye, as one of the two coastal states of the Aegean Sea, remains ready to cooperate with Greece.
“Within the framework of the Athens Declaration on 'Good Neighborly Relations' of Dec. 7, 2023, Türkiye maintains its position that a sincere and comprehensive approach should be adopted to resolve problems on the basis of international law, equity and good-neighborliness,” Keceli added.

Europe, UN rally behind ICC after new US sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
18:26:00 UTC
03:26:00 KST

European governments, EU leaders and the U.N. rallied behind the International Criminal Court on Wednesday, condemning a new round of U.S. sanctions targeting senior court officials and warning that mounting pressure on the tribunal threatens the independence of international justice.
The latest U.S. measures target ICC President Tomoko Akane of Japan and Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal, a senior trial lawyer in the Office of the Prosecutor.
The sanctions are part of a broader pressure campaign against the Hague-based court launched by U.S. President Donald Trump's administration. Tensions have escalated since the ICC issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes in Gaza.
U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres voiced "serious concern" regarding the U.S. decision to impose sanctions on high-ranking ICC officials.
"The secretary-general expresses serious concern about this designation, as well as the ongoing designation of other International Criminal Court employees," spokesperson Stephane Dujarric told reporters on Wednesday.
He emphasized that the U.N. views the ICC as a "key pillar of international criminal justice" and maintains full respect for its operations.
France condemned the measures and expressed solidarity with the officials targeted.
"France condemns all forms of threats and means of coercion taken against the Court, its staff and the civil society organisations which support it," the French Foreign Ministry said, adding that Paris stood in solidarity with the targeted judges.
U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk also called on Washington to immediately lift the sanctions.
Türk described the measures as unacceptable and urged governments to defend institutions established to uphold human rights and the rule of law, while protecting court officials facing reprisals.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa similarly threw their support behind the ICC, saying its judges and officials must be able to carry out their work independently and without external pressure.
They stressed that the court plays a key role in delivering justice to victims of some of the world's gravest crimes.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas reaffirmed the bloc's "unwavering support" for the ICC, describing it as a cornerstone of the international criminal justice system and the global fight against impunity.
Kallas warned that sanctions against the court and its personnel undermine its work and said the EU would continue supporting efforts to protect the institution and its staff from external pressure, intimidation and interference.
Britain also reiterated its support for the ICC's independence, saying those responsible for the most serious international crimes must be held accountable.
Germany said protecting the court as an independent institution remained of central importance, while acknowledging that the ICC, like other institutions, could legitimately face criticism.
Spain went further, describing the U.S. measures as a "flagrant attack" on the court's independence, integrity and impartiality and emphasizing its role in securing accountability for serious crimes and justice for victims.
The Netherlands also rejected the latest sanctions, with Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen stressing that international courts and tribunals must be allowed to carry out their mandates freely.
The ICC itself strongly rejected the new U.S. measures Wednesday, calling them "flagrant attacks" on judicial independence.
According to the court, nine of its 18 judges, both deputy prosecutors, its former prosecutor and one staff member are now subject to U.S. sanctions.
The latest measures stem from sanctions against the ICC imposed by Trump in February 2025 amid Washington's opposition to the court's actions involving Israel.

Zelensky fires senior aide amid anti-corruption scandal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
18:25:11 UTC
03:25:11 KST

Zelensky fires senior aide amid anti-corruption scandal
Ukraine's Vladimir Zelensky has fired Irina Mudraya, deputy head of his office, after media reports indicated that her home was raided as part of anti-corruption probe over alleged money laundering scheme.
The Western-supported National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) announced on Wednesday that it and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) were targeting an alleged criminal organization led by a current and former lawmaker and involving senior officials from Zelensky’s office.
NABU later said members of the alleged group had laundered 150 million hryvnia ($3.3 million) in cash through shell-company accounts to finance bail for a defendant in the Midas investigation. That sprawling corruption case centers in part on an alleged $100 million embezzlement and kickback scheme involving the country’s nuclear operator Energoatom, which investigators say was masterminded by Timur Mindich, a longtime business associate of Zelensky.
While NABU did not name the suspects, ZN.ua, citing law-enforcement sources, identified them as Mudraya, lawmaker Vadim Stolar, and ex-MP Maksim Mikitas, adding that several Justice Ministry officials and Sense Bank representatives were also targeted.
As for the defendant in need of bail, Ukrainian media identified him as former Energy Minister German Galushchenko, who was fired after the Midas scandal broke and detained as he attempted to flee the country.
Recordings released by NABU featured discussions about moving the bail funds and avoiding scrutiny. In one excerpt, an unidentified woman – potentially Mudraya – cites another unidentified person as saying, “corruption needs to be systematized and controlled, not fought.” Another voice adds: “and led.”
The scandal is part of several high-level graft cases. Earlier this month, anti-corruption authorities accused former ambassador to the US Olga Stefanishina of illicit enrichment and inaccurate asset declarations. Last month, they also accused several senior officials in Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry of large-scale fraud, embezzlement, and money laundering aimed at stealing foreign money.
Rampant corruption in Ukraine has long been the case, and only intensified after the escalation of Kiev’s conflict with Russia in 2022. EU officials have also designated graft as one of Ukraine’s key obstacles to membership.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has said that “corruption in Ukraine has become a byword” as it “permeates the entire Ukrainian power structure, including Zelensky’s inner circle and Zelensky himself.”

MOSCOW, August 19. /TASS/. Ukraine plans to legalize the disposal of thousands of bodies of soldiers listed as missing as surgical waste, a Russian security source told TASS.
