Jellyfish the stars at Florida museum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
16:38:23 UTC
01:38:23 KST

The floating tentacled predators pulse and swirl in hypnotic patterns in the dark museum space, lit primarily by images projected on the walls and the glowing light from the saltwater tanks.
The private Jellyfish Museum in Pompano Beach, Florida, is believed to be the first museum in the US dedicated solely to the translucent invertebrates and one of the few such spaces in the world, city and the museum’s founders said.
It was created by Alex and Yana Yanovsky, who previously developed successful aquariums in Ukraine, including their first jellyfish museum in Kyiv. The couple left those facilities behind when they fled Ukraine following the 2022 Russian invasion, operations manager Jessica Eisenbarth said.
Photo: AP
The museum, which opened in the spring, is the couple’s first aquatic attraction since immigrating to the US, but they would like to expand.
“When they left Ukraine, they moved to Florida, and then they immediately wanted to share their passion here,” Eisenbarth said.
Jellyfish have no heart or brain, and are made up primarily of water, giving them a translucent look.
Yana Yanovsky came up with the idea for the jellyfish museum after noticing how popular the jellyfish were at their other aquariums.
“Jellyfish are some of the most resilient creatures on Earth. While they lack a brain, they maintain a simple nerve net that allows them to respond to their environment,” Yana said in a statement provided by the city. “Their movement is mesmerizing, almost meditative, and they play an important role in marine ecosystems.”
Smithsonian Environmental Research Center director Monty Graham said he is not surprised someone made an aquarium dedicated to jellyfish.
He credits the Monterey Bay Aquarium in California with starting the popularity of jellyfish exhibits at aquariums all over the world.
Monterey Bay Aquarium began displaying jellyfish in temporary exhibits in 1985 and opened a permanent gallery in 1996.
“Jellyfish are cool, they’re things that people don’t get to see up close unless they’re scuba diving,” Graham said. “So here was this opportunity, in a controlled environment, very beautiful settings.”
The nearly 900m2 Jellyfish Museum houses about 20 unique species of jellyfish found in Florida waters and other parts of the world. Different species can be rotated through the museum’s 21 tanks. Some occupants include Japanese sea nettles, moon jellyfish, spotted jellies and upside-down jellyfish, the last of which can be found among Florida’s mangrove swamps.
The space is designed to exude calm and tranquility, general manager Iryna Pelypkanych said.
It was converted from a former Wells Fargo bank branch with about US$100,000 in community redevelopment grants from the city of Pompano Beach. Guides teach people about the role jellyfish play in marine ecosystems and the importance of protecting them.
“The biggest idea here is to leave people with the feeling that they know something more about the population of jellyfish,” Pelypkanych said. “Because so far, we know around 4,000 different species that can be called jellyfish.”

Fairchild to receive Taiwan Employment Gold Card in public ceremony
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
16:38:23 UTC
01:38:23 KST

Taiwanese-American baseball player Stuart Fairchild’s application for a Taiwan Employment Gold Card has been approved, a senior National Development Council (NDC) official said Wednesday.
The NDC and Ministry of Sports are planning a public ceremony in November to formally present Fairchild with the card, NDC Deputy Minister Peng Li-pei (彭立沛) said.
Fairchild, affectionately nicknamed “Feizai” (費仔) by Taiwanese fans, represented Taiwan at the World Baseball Classic (WBC) in March and was eligible to play for the country through his Taiwanese mother.
Photo: Taipei Times
The 30-year-old outfielder drew widespread attention for his performance during the tournament, hitting home runs and driving in key runs that made him a fan favorite in Taiwan.
Fairchild recently became a free agent after a brief stint in the Seattle Mariners organization.
Following his strong performance in the WBC, the NDC reached out to encourage him to apply for the card, a four- in-one document that combines an open work permit, resident visa, Alien Resident Certificate (ARC) and re-entry permit in a single smart card valid for one to three years.
The Gold Card program was launched in 2018 under the Act for the Recruitment and Employment of Foreign Professionals to attract and retain overseas talent by providing a more flexible work and residency framework.
The program targets foreign professionals with expertise in fields including technology, economics, education, arts and culture, sports, finance, law, architecture, national defense and digital technology, as well as others recognized by the authorities as possessing special expertise.
Responding to a question from Kuomintang lawmaker Lu Yu-ling (呂玉玲) during a legislative hearing about the status of Fairchild’s application, Peng said the review had been completed and that the NDC and Sports Ministry were arranging a public ceremony to jointly present Fairchild with the card.
Lu said that while more than 10,000 Employment Gold Cards have been issued to date, relatively few have gone to applicants in the sports field. She asked whether the eligibility threshold was too high or whether applicants simply did not meet the requirements.
Deputy Sports Minister Huang Chi-huang (黃啟煌) said the eligibility criteria for sports-related applicants have gradually expanded, allowing not only athletes but also sports science researchers and data analysts to apply.
Huang said Taiwan is currently seeking more sports support professionals, particularly specialists in sports data analysis.
The Sports Ministry plans to hold another meeting on Aug. 27 to discuss further easing the eligibility criteria in an effort to lower barriers and attract more international talent, he added.

Geneva envoy probe could take months: minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
16:38:22 UTC
01:38:22 KST

An investigation into Taiwan’s representative in Geneva, Greg Lee (李冠德), could take two months given the extensive allegations against him, Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) said yesterday.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs received a signed complaint late last month accusing Lee of workplace bullying, poor leadership and the use of public resources for personal purposes, Lin said at a meeting of the legislature’s Foreign Affairs and National Defense Committee.
A special investigative task force was formed on Aug. 2 and includes people from outside the ministry with legal expertise, he said.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
“We are relying on the task force to clarify the facts. We also hope they can speed up the investigation, but we cannot jump to conclusions before the final results are released,” he said.
Given the extent of the allegations, the investigation would also involve different ministry departments, he added.
If the investigation concludes that Lee engaged in workplace bullying, he would be asked to leave his post in Geneva and return to the ministry’s headquarters in Taipei for further review and possible disciplinary action, Personnel Department Director Lu Shih-yi (呂世壹) said.
Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Legislator Hsu Chiao-hsin (徐巧芯) said that in eight of the 10 workplace-bullying complaints involving the ministry’s headquarters and overseas offices since Lin took office in May 2024, seven had been closed with no disciplinary action taken.
The eighth is the investigation into Lee.
Lee’s case became public earlier this month after Taiwanese media reported that staff at the Geneva office had jointly filed a 15-page complaint accompanied by a 134-page dossier detailing alleged misconduct.
Among the allegations was that Lee verbally humiliated subordinates and that his management style caused some employees to seek medical help.
Lee has also been accused of spending about NT$130,000 in public funds on high-end chocolates for visiting Taiwanese lawmakers attending events in Geneva last year, and of later asking subordinates to submit false expense claims to cover the expenses.
Lee has reportedly returned to Taipei, but Lin said the investigative team had yet to interview him.
In a separate exchange, KMT Legislator Lai Shyh-bao (賴士葆) asked Lin to comment on what Lai described as the ministry’s “soft” remarks on visits by senior members of Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s Cabinet to the Yasukuni Shrine in Tokyo last week.
The visits drew diplomatic protests and strong condemnation from China and South Korea.
However, the ministry only expressed respect for different views in Japan regarding the visits by Takaichi’s Cabinet members, drawing criticism from the KMT and the Taiwan People’s Party, which described the response as weak.
Lin said the government “respects” the diversity of views in Japan regarding senior officials’ visits to the controversial shrine honoring Japan’s war dead, including World War II war criminals, but also hopes Tokyo would reflect on its wartime aggression.
“We recognize and respect the diversity of views within Japanese society regarding these issues. We look forward to [Japan’s] continuous reflection — ensuring that the crime of waging war is never repeated — while also anticipating joint efforts [between Taipei and Tokyo] to uphold regional peace and stability,” he said at the legislature in Taipei.
“We hope that current Taiwan-Japan relations will contribute to peace in the region,” he added.

Tech expo comes to Taipei, showing us the future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
16:38:20 UTC
01:38:20 KST

Intelligent Asia, Taiwan’s largest industrial exhibition and a major platform for artificial intelligence (AI), robotics and automation, opened yesterday at the Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center.
The exhibition features about 1,200 vendors from 16 countries and regions across 4,500 booths across halls 1 and 2, showcasing advanced technologies including AI-powered robots, automation equipment and smart logistics, event organizers said.
The expo, which runs through Saturday, showcases key technologies required for humanoid robots, including AI computing, visual recognition, sensing systems, motion control, power supplies, servo motors and joint actuators, organizers said.
This year’s event — which encompasses the Taiwan Automation Intelligence and Robot Show and the Taipei International Industrial Automation Exhibition — highlights the nation’s robotics supply chain, including Solomon Technology Corp (所羅門), Techman Robot Inc (達明機器人), Advantech Co (研華), Nexcom International Co (新漢), Swancor Robotech Co (上緯智聯), Aurotek Corp (和椿科技) and Chieftek Precision Co (直得科技).
At the show, Coretronic Intelligent Logistics Solutions Corp (中光電智能物流) is showcasing its autonomous mobile robot carrier and forklift.
Coretronic Intelligent senior project manager Ritz Chang (張明儒) said the carrier could be used in a wide range of settings, such as unloading cargo at ports, delivering patients’ medical records in hospitals or delivering food.
Several food delivery services in the US are deploying thousands of AI-driven delivery couriers, Chang said.
“They are replacing food couriers in the United States because low birthrates are a global trend, and wages are high in the States,” Chang said.
“[AI-driven delivery couriers] also don’t feel tired, and they offer more scheduling flexibility,” he said.
Hiwin Technologies Corp (上銀科技) is displaying a humanoid robot designed to supply components in supply chains, as well as an eight-axis robotic arm capable of making sophisticated movements in confined spaces such as containers.
Hiwin deputy general manager Kyle Wong (翁振民) said the company developed the robots in anticipation of greater automation in the logistics sector.
“Since the job mainly involves loading and unloading goods and is very repetitive and monotonous, fewer and fewer people will want to do this kind of work in the future,” Wong said. “So, we are developing these robots primarily to take over this kind of boring and repetitive work.”
Swancor Robotech, a subsidiary of Swancor Holding Co (上緯投控), is demonstrating the capacity of the company’s quadrupedal robot at the event.
The company said it plans to launch a robot dog fully designed and developed in Taiwan, dubbed the "Taiwanese native dog," by the middle of next year.
Local assembly is expected to begin by the end of this year, as the company aims to develop core technologies including the robot’s "brain," control systems and joint modules, moving beyond its current role as an importer and distributor, it said.
Swancor said its robot dogs can perform autonomous navigation, image recognition, voice commands and environmental sensing for applications including power facility and factory inspections. They can also climb stairs and overcome obstacles.
Swancor Holding chairman Robert Tsai (蔡朝陽) said the company estimates Taiwan’s annual robot dog market at more than 3,000 units, worth NT$2 billion to NT$3 billion (US$62 million to US$93 million).
The government is also developing a domestic quadrupedal robot platform. The Industrial Technology Research Institute has worked with Compal Electronics Inc (仁寶), Inventec Corp (英業達) and Solomon Technology Corp (所羅門) to develop robots for firefighting, security and infrastructure inspections.
Those developments were made possible thanks to a platform that allows domestic companies to test and replace key components, including motors, visual sensors and joints, to build a local robotics supply chain and combine Taiwan’s hardware strengths with AI and software, according to the Ministry of Economic Affairs.

Taiwan needs both nuclear and renewable power, trade group says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
16:38:19 UTC
01:38:19 KST

Taiwan should pursue nuclear and renewable power together to ensure a stable electricity supply as the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) drives demand for computing infrastructure and electricity. Third Wednesday Club chairman Lin Por-fong (林伯豐) said yesterday.
“Without a stable supply of electricity, there can be no industrial development,” Lin said on the sidelines of the trade group’s monthly gathering in Taipei.
High solar-power costs and difficulties in developing offshore wind made it necessary to reconsider the country’s energy policy, said Lin, who is also chairman of Taiwan Glass Industry Corp (台玻).
Photo: CNA
Taiwan Power Co’s (Taipower, 台電) accumulated losses, which stood at NT$376.4 billion (US$11.78 billion) at the end of June, cannot be addressed simply through higher electricity rates or government subsidies, he said.
The government-convened electricity rate review committee is due to meet next month to decide whether to adjust electricity rates or extend the current freeze, as Taiwan seeks to cushion the impact of rising energy costs on domestic inflation.
Lin said raising electricity rates or relying on government subsidies would not address the underlying problem. Instead, policymakers should seek to lower power-generation costs by expanding nuclear power, which he estimated costs about NT$1 per kilowatt-hour, compared with an overall generation cost approaching NT$3.
Taiwan has sought to expand renewable energy, while phasing out nuclear power, but the transition has faced higher-than-expected costs and difficulties in offshore wind development. Some offshore wind operators have also encountered financial difficulties, Lin said.
The issue is becoming more urgent as Taiwan’s AI industry expands and power consumption accelerates, he said.
Lin also backed an increase in Taiwan’s minimum wage, saying that higher minimum wages could lift overall pay levels but arguing that minimum wages for local and foreign migrant workers should be decoupled.
Domestic workers should receive higher pay based on differences in work performance and employment conditions, he said.
Taiwan’s minimum monthly wage is expected to exceed NT$30,000 next year, up from NT$29,500.
Wage increases are an inevitable trend amid strong economic growth, Lin said. However, the government should consider whether traditional industries could absorb higher labor costs as they continue to face difficulties, he said.
Taiwan’s labor authorities are due to review the minimum wage next month.

The United Arab Emirates (UAE) on Tuesday said that it is suspending all trade and financial dealings with Iran after reporting an Iranian missile attack directed at its ships.
The announcement comes after a period of relative calm in the UAE, with no Iranian missiles aimed at the country since May after it bore the brunt of attacks in the early weeks of the Middle East war.
However, Abu Dhabi has accused Tehran of repeatedly targeting its tankers at sea in the past few weeks.
Photo: AP
“In light of regional escalations ... all trade, commercial exchanges, and financial transactions with Iran have been halted until further notice,” UAE Ministry of Foreign Communications Director Afra al-Hameli said.
Abu Dhabi accused Iran of firing two ballistic missiles toward the country.
It later said the salvo was directed at shipping, but Tehran denied firing missiles at the UAE.
“UAE air defenses detected two ballistic missiles launched from Iran towards the country, with the first falling outside the country’s territorial waters, while the second fell within the territorial waters,” the ministry said in a statement posted on social media.
A second statement released later said the missiles “were targeting maritime navigation and fell into the sea.”
Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei “categorically rejected the United Arab Emirates’ claim that Iran had launched a missile towards that country,” calling it harmful to regional trust and security efforts.
The first UAE statement came nearly two hours after a phone alert that warned residents of a “potential missile threat.”
The UAE is home to a sizeable Iranian community and has been a major trading partner for US-sanctioned Iran, at least before the war.
They share deep cultural and historical ties as neighboring countries across the Gulf, with centuries-old links between coastal communities, trade routes and family networks.
Tuesday’s announcement is the latest measure against Iran by the UAE after it recalled its ambassador early in the conflict, and shut Iran-linked schools and a hospital.
At the height of the war in March, authorities ordered the closure of an Iranian state-linked hospital in Dubai, three employees at the facility told reporters, with schools and a community center also ordered closed.
A UAE official told reporters at the time that “certain institutions directly linked to the Iranian regime and IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] will be closed under targeted measures” after they were found to have contravened UAE laws.

Rain is expected across Taiwan from Thursday through the weekend under the influence of a low-pressure system, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) said Wednesday.
Southern Taiwan and mountainous areas of central and eastern Taiwan could see localized heavy or torrential rain during this period, while northern Taiwan may experience localized heavy rain and brief periods of intense rainfall in the afternoons, CWA forecaster Chang Cheng-chuan (張承傳) told reporters.
Chang said seasonal southwesterly winds will strengthen from Friday through Sunday, bringing more frequent showers and thundershowers to central and southern Taiwan that could prompt heavy rain advisories.
Photo: CNA
Localized heavy rain is also expected in northern Taiwan and other parts of the island, he said.
The low-pressure system is expected to move away from Taiwan after Monday next week, but central, southern and southeastern Taiwan could still see rain that day. Afternoon thundershowers are forecast in southern areas on Tuesday and Wednesday, Chang said.
Due to the rain, daily highs in southern Taiwan will remain around 31-32 degrees Celsius, while temperatures elsewhere will reach around 33-35 degrees, he said.
Photo grab from CWA website
Meanwhile, a tropical depression southeast of Guam strengthened into Tropical Storm Saudel at 2 p.m. Wednesday, according to the CWA.
Chang said Saudel remains far from Taiwan and is forecast to move northwest before turning west-northwest. Although the storm is expected to approach waters near Okinawa on Monday, uncertainty over its future path remains high and its potential impact on Taiwan is unclear, he said.
Saudel is also expected to strengthen further in the coming days, Chang said.

Notes from Central Taiwan: The blockade Taiwan is not ready for
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
16:38:11 UTC
01:38:11 KST

An interesting essay in the spring issue this year of International Security by Kerby Davis and Eugene Gholz explores the possibilities and outcomes of simulated missile attacks by the People’s Republic of China (PRC) on Taiwan’s ports to carry out a blockade.
“Substantively,” they conclude in Blockade by Fire: China’s Potential to Blockade Taiwan Using Missile Attacks on Ports, “our article raises serious concern about Taiwan’s vulnerability to Chinese military coercion. Even if Taiwan and the United States take steps to better prepare for a Chinese blockade, they face a greater threat from China than analysts previously believed.”
The authors see the missile blockade as a better choice for Beijing than a traditional ship-based blockade.
Their models look at a wide range of variables, including missile types, target types (cranes, cranes and ships in harbor, etc), and what rules the PRC will use to govern its choices. In their baseline scenario, the PRC aims to reduce cargo throughput in the ports to 25 percent of its pre-strike level. Hence, whenever a port recovers to 25 percent of its normal activity, the PRC launches a fresh wave of missiles. Other scenarios assume constant firing of missiles. Cranes are key targets because it is difficult to unload cargo from large ships without them, and they are hard to replace. It should be noted that the dominant global maker of cranes, Zhenhua Heavy Industries, is a firm based in Shanghai.
“But considering the mix of costs and benefits,” the authors contend, “the continual-firing strategy using DF-11As, targeting only cranes, and offsetting the aimpoints inland, away from ships, looks dangerously promising from the Chinese perspective.”
The authors recommend that Taiwan adopt responses to this scenario.
Photo: Hung Ting-hung, Taipei Times
Davis and Gholz observe that Taiwan does have large shipping firms such as Wan Hai Lines Ltd (萬海航運) and Evergreen Marine Corp (長榮海運) that could easily supply ships to run a blockade. But having access to ships is not the same thing as having crews willing to sail them into a combat zone. Taiwanese carriers employ multinational crews, and seafarer availability could become an important constraint. Few commentators writing on blockade scenarios have considered the problem of crewing the ships that are supposed to run the blockade, though media reports of crews refusing Black Sea assignments are common.
“Fear of being killed, rather than merely caught in the crossfire, is prompting experienced officers to refuse Black Sea assignments as attacks on merchant shipping intensify,” Lloyd’s List reported last month. Davis and Gholz point out that the PRC will also be actively chartering crews and ships to hinder their use as blockade runners, a common tactic in blockades during war.
The authors do discuss the Russian attacks on Ukraine Black Sea ports, which failed to knock them out. Moreover, once international shippers realized the risk was low and manageable, they continued to send in ships. Russia’s efforts to close the ports via naval surface blockade and missile attacks have thus far not been completely successful, though as recent media reports show, they are having an effect.
Photo courtesy of Evergreen Marine Corp
There are few other examples of major ports being knocked out by missile attacks in the modern era, but in fact in the 1971 India-Pakistan War, in Operations Trident and Python, Indian missile boats armed with Russian Styx missiles hit the port of Karachi, destroying several ships in port and setting major fuel-storage facilities ablaze. The loss of the fuel tanks (also hit by air raids) badly disrupted Pakistan’s principal port, along with billions in repair costs. This damage was applied with a handful of relatively unsophisticated missiles.
One interesting aspect of Indian naval ownership of the sea around Pakistan is that after the second Indian attack on the port, a de facto Indian blockade arose. Initially, neutral ships sought safe passage from the Indian authorities before heading to Karachi. Later, commercial traffic to Karachi largely dried up.
The political implications of a Taiwan blockade by fire raised by the Indian success with Karachi are obvious. If neutral carriers felt compelled to seek Chinese assurances or safe passage before entering Taiwanese ports, Beijing could exploit those requests as evidence that it exercised effective control over access to Taiwan — even though requesting safe conduct would not itself constitute recognition of Chinese sovereignty. The purpose of a blockade by fire may thus include this political goal. Davis and Gholz note that one advantage of missile attacks is they don’t take place in the land, sea, or air space of other nations, playing to PRC propaganda that Taiwan is an “internal” matter.
The Davis and Gholz paper focuses on the direct effects of strikes on Taiwan’s ports. What happens to Taiwan’s other industries? They note that the last round of PRC drill simulated attacks on ports and energy facilities. If missiles start landing on Taiwan’s ports, what happens to the migrant workers that Taiwan depends on to run its tech and construction industries? Will they remain? Does the government have a “danger pay” policy? Does it plan to compel migrant workers to remain in Taiwan?
Many of Taiwan’s highest-value semiconductor shipments leave by air. Shipments of chips will continue until stockpiles run out, if the airports are open. If they are open, people — from migrant workers to engineers to executives — will want to flee. Ukraine has suffered severe losses of workers, both through flight and through people entering the military, seriously impeding its recovery efforts. So will Taiwan. The PRC could theoretically leave the airports functioning for just that reason.
Further, construction workers will be at a premium if Taiwan needs to quickly repair its ports. The Taiwan International Ports Corp, the state-owned firm that owns the ports, had a total workforce of 2,086 workers in 2024, all but nine full-time, and another 389 workers under contract. That is far too small a workforce to carry out rapid, major repairs on half a dozen international ports all at once. Workforce strain will become acute if construction workers must clear ports and fix energy facilities simultaneously.
Taiwan’s much-touted resilience?
“Taiwan’s military and homeland security organizations have not organized exercises with port operators to practice responses to national security emergencies,” Davis and Gholz dolefully observe, based on interviews from June 2024.
Neither Taiwan’s shipping firms nor the Taiwan International Ports Corporation have practiced scenarios involving destruction at the ports, nor have they reserves of parts and equipment for that, they learned from their interviews.
That NT$10,000 AI industry dividend that the administration of William Lai (賴清德) and the Legislature take turns promising to the public would be much better spent on creating rapid response engineering and repair teams, drills for port attacks and repairs and practicing the logistical headaches of shifting workers out of Taiwan’s endless apartment construction and into port clearing and repairs.
We may need them soon.
Notes from Central Taiwan is a column written by long-term resident Michael Turton, who provides incisive commentary informed by three decades of living in and writing about his adoptive country. The views expressed here are his own.

It was Aug. 18, 1945, three days after Japan announced its surrender to the Allies. Bose, who advocated armed struggle to free India from British rule, had worked closely with Imperial Japan. He was attempting to reach the Soviet Union via Manchuria in the hope of gaining support

No injuries reported from explosion of test rocket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
16:38:11 UTC
01:38:11 KST

A satellite launch vehicle being tested for the first time was detonated after an anomaly shortly after liftoff, but no injuries or property damage were reported, the National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology said in a statement yesterday.
The test of the Taiwan-made launch vehicle was conducted yesterday morning at the institute’s Jioupeng Base (九鵬基地) in a sparsely populated area of eastern Pingtung County.
The rocket deviated from its intended trajectory during the initial stage of flight, prompting operators to activate its self-destruct mechanism in line with established emergency procedures, it said.
Photo courtesy of a member of the public
The destruction of the rocket confined the debris to a safe zone, it said.
Notices issued by the institute before the test said that it had scheduled sea and air weapon firing exercises at the Jioupeng area from yesterday to tomorrow, including artillery fire and uncrewed aircraft system operations.
The notice said the danger zone covered an area within a 20 nautical mile (37km) radius, with a maximum altitude of 100,000 feet (30.48km).
It was the first time the Taiwan-developed launch vehicle had been tested.
The institute issued the statement after Chinese-language media reported that residents near the test site saw the craft veer off course shortly after launch before crashing into a mountainous area, raising concern among nearby communities.
The Pingtung County Government in a separate statement called on the institute to immediately suspend launch tests, review its launch procedures, and adjust future flight paths to avoid indigenous villages and other residential areas.
The institute said no injuries or property damage were reported.
It would review telemetry data collected during the test and revise the vehicle’s design accordingly, it said.

National preparedness is important
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
16:38:09 UTC
01:38:09 KST

I was in Taichung when this year’s urban resilience exercises began in central Taiwan on Monday last week.
For the first time, the air raid drills included a mobile Internet “throttling” scenario. This did not mean that mobile Internet was entirely cut off; rather it simulated limited communications through measures such as slowing mobile networks.
Before the exercises began, authorities advised people who needed Internet access to use fixed-line connections or indoor Wi-Fi.
For most people, a half hour of slower Internet would, at most, amount to a minor inconvenience in their daily lives.
It is hard not to wonder: If I was in Kyiv, Moscow, Tehran or Tel Aviv, would slower Internet really be the only thing I have to worry about?
A real air raid would not be announced in advance, nor would it last just 30 minutes. When air raid sirens sound, people could be confronted with explosions, power outages, communication disruptions and even threats to their lives. Seen in this light, the inconvenience people in Taichung experienced was a small price to pay.
It is for this reason that I commend the armed forces, government agencies, the Ministry of Digital Affairs, the National Communications Commission and the telecoms that took part in the exercises. It is precisely because people are willing to prepare, conduct drills and coordinate during peacetime that they know what to do when communications are restricted, even in calm environments.
With the advent of high-tech tactics and strategies, the battlefield is no longer simply about guns and ammunition. The Internet, communications and essential services could all affect the functioning of society. Taiwan cannot predict what methods adversaries would employ, but at the very least, it can ensure the nation is prepared.
This is not just a matter for the military. The government must clearly define responsibilities, businesses must maintain essential services and the public must know what they can do when a crisis occurs. The more Taiwanese understand and practice during peacetime, the less likely they are to panic when a crisis strikes.
In peaceful times, these exercises inevitably bring some inconvenience to our daily lives, but if that inconvenience leads to greater preparedness when a real crisis strikes, it is worth it. We do not know what we might face, but there is one thing we can do: Ensure that Taiwan is prepared.
Hung Yu-jui is a translator and Japanese-language teacher based in Taiwan who writes on public policy and social issues.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

Mom and daughter become first Siraya people registered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
16:38:08 UTC
01:38:08 KST

A mother and daughter in Tainan have become the first people to complete their official registration as Siraya after the government on July 30 recognized Siraya as Taiwan’s 17th indigenous group.
The registration of the mother, Mai Fang-chi (買方祺), and daughter, Shih Ya-hsin (石亞欣), was completed yesterday at Tainan’s South District Household Registration Office and witnessed by Tainan Mayor Huang Wei-che (黃偉哲), the city said in a statement.
Huang said the registration marked an important milestone for Siraya, who have long sought recognition of their identity and place in history after preserving and passing down their culture in Tainan for generations.
Photo courtesy of the Tainan City Government
Tainan’s household registration offices began accepting applications for Siraya identification on Thursday last week, after the Council of Indigenous Peoples announced the eligibility criteria the same day, the statement said.
As of Tuesday, the offices had received 1,545 applications, of which 10 of the first 12 applications reviewed met the requirements, the city government said.
Of the 10, Mai and Shih were the first to go to the office to complete their registration.
Tainan has since 2005 recognized the indigenous status of people seen as “assimilated indigenous peoples.”
Under the new system, those who complete the registration process would receive “Plains indigenous” status recognized under national law, the city said.
The eligibility requirements for Siraya registration lean heavily on precedent.
Applicants or their direct ancestors have to have been registered as “Plains” or assimilated indigenous peoples under Japanese rule (1895 to 1945), and they had to be registered as living in Siraya regions during that time period.
If that is not an option, applicants must present other evidence of their indigenous Taiwanese ancestry dating back to the Japanese colonial period.
Siraya are the first “Plains” indigenous group to be officially recognized by the government, following the legislature’s passage of the Pingpu Indigenous People’s Status Act (平埔原住民族群身分法) in October last year.
Also referred to as “assimilated indigenous peoples” during the Japanese colonial period, “Plains” indigenous peoples have struggled to gain recognition because they were deemed to have largely become Sinicized.
As a result, the government previously officially recognized only “highland” indigenous tribes.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) last month said that eight other “Plains” indigenous groups had submitted applications for recognition that were awaiting review by the council.

Techman Robot Inc (達明機器人) yesterday showcased its new TM45S heavy-load dual-arm collaborative robots for artificial intelligence (AI) server assembly and semiconductor handling at the Taipei International Industrial Automation Exhibition amid rising demand.
Each arm can carry up to 50kg, or 100kg combined, allowing the system to handle AI servers and other heavy components, Techman chief operating officer Scott Huang (黃識忠) said.
TM45S’ built-in vision positioning allows it to adjust its pick-and-place position automatically when components shift, he said.
Photo: Fang Wei-chieh, Taipei Times
The product is in the proof-of-concept (POC) stage at server and chipmaking production lines, with sales set to begin by the end of this year and customer deliveries to start in the first quarter of next year, he said.
Techman is a subsidiary of Quanta Computer Inc (廣達電腦). It operates a manufacturing facility in New Taipei City’s Linkou District (林口), with customers spanning semiconductors, automotive components and traditional industries such as textiles.
The company plans to provide its TM Xplore I humanoid robot, showcased last year, to select customers for development and testing in the second half of this year, with commercial sales likely next year, Huang said.
As safety and cybersecurity remain hurdles for humanoid robots in factories, particularly in Europe and the US where regulations are stricter, and training dexterous robotic hands is still a major technical challenge, Techman plans to develop a second-generation humanoid robot to improve safety and better meet industrial requirements, he said.
Commenting on the successful listing of Chinese robot maker Unitree Robotics (宇樹科技) on the Shanghai stock exchange yesterday, Huang said companies need to build on their own strengths. Unitree has strong motion-control technology, while US companies still lead in higher-level AI capabilities, he said.
Techman’s strengths lie in accumulating industrial know-how and meeting practical customer needs, Huang said.
The company’s Taiwan-based manufacturing and largely non-China supply chain could provide an advantage as US and Japanese customers seek to reduce reliance on Chinese suppliers, he said.
Techman president Haw Chen (陳尚昊) said the company’s business performance in the second half is expected to outperform the first half.
Semiconductor and electronics applications remain Techman’s main revenue sources, and about 90 percent of its autonomous mobile robot (AMR) applications are semiconductor-related, Techman vice president William Wang (王偉霖) said.
Products combining AMRs with collaborative robots accounted for about 30 percent of its NT$1.14 billion (US$35.7 million) revenue in the first seven months of this year, Wang said.

Asked to clarify what the third category of combat unit was, the Ministry of National Defense said that the definition of combat unit was broadened in recognition of the vital contributions specialists make in sustaining the military’s ability to fight.
According to the joint warfare concept, medical services; logistics; chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear defense forces; and military police units play mission-critical roles in supporting front-line units, the ministry said.
Maintenance and repair, training, research and development, military intelligence and psychological warfare units are included in the expanded definition for creating and maintaining combat power, it said.
The new category also includes personnel serving in brigades whose subunits already have combat troop designations, as well as those guarding key infrastructure, it said.
Military personnel in infantry, armor, artillery, air defense or Marine companies, as well as maritime surface combatants and submarine crews are Category 1 combat troops who receive a NT$12,000 monthly bonus, it said.
Category 2 combat troops, who receive a NT$7,000 bonus, are those that support fighting companies or navy vessels, it added.

Unknown

16:38:03 UTC
01:38:03 KST

A demographic study showed that 28.9 percent of Taiwanese who have never been married have also never been in a romantic relationship, and up to 69.68 percent are not currently in a relationship.
The 2024 Panel Study of Family Dynamics, led by Academia Sinica research fellow Yu Ruoh-rong (于若蓉) and funded by the National Science and Technology Council, is the latest wave of a long-running study that began in 1999 and has gathered data over three generations as part of the wider Taiwan Empirical Survey Data.
To mark the Qixi Festival yesterday, also known as Lovers’ Day, the Taiwan Empirical Survey Data posted on Facebook an analysis of results from the 2024 survey about dating habits among 1,712 Taiwanese who have never been married.
Photo: Wang Chu-hsiu, Taipei Times
Of those surveyed, 30.32 percent were in relationships, 40.78 percent were single after having been in a relationship before, and 28.9 percent had always been single.
Of men surveyed, 28.26 percent said they had been single their whole life, while the rate was 30.11 percent for women, showing little relative gender difference, the survey found.
Compared across different age groups, 30.1 percent of respondents aged 27 to 31 had never been in a relationship, compared with 27.8 percent of those aged 32 to 36, 27.7 percent of those aged 37 to 41, 29.2 percent of people aged 42 to 46, 30.8 percent of 47 to 51-year-olds and 28.6 percent of those 52 or older.
The survey data showed that 44.3 percent of 27 to 31-year-olds who have never married said they were in a relationship, compared with just 8.9 percent of people 52 and older, with the percentage of people in a relationship decreasing steadily throughout the age groups.

US sanctions ICC president, trial lawyer to dismantle the international body
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
16:38:03 UTC
01:38:03 KST

US sanctions ICC president, trial lawyer to dismantle the international body
The US announced on Tuesday that it is sanctioning the Japanese president of the International Criminal Court (ICC), Tomoko Akane, as well as the body's Senegalese senior trial lawyer, Abdoulaye Seye.
The move is just the latest step in implementing US President Donald Trump's stated mission of dismantling the ICC for investigating Israeli and, potentially, US officials for war crimes, Middle East Eye reported.
Neither country is a signatory to the Rome Statute, which established the court in 2002.
There are, however, 125 countries that are ICC member states, several of which have been roiled by extrajudicial US and Israeli military action.
"The Trump Administration has been clear: the ICC is a corrupt and fatally politicized supranational court that has maliciously abused its authority and exceeded its mandate. We will not tolerate its assault on state sovereignty," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement.
Akane and Seye, he added, "have directly engaged in efforts by the ICC to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC jurisdiction... This sets a dangerous precedent for all nations".
Just days after he assumed power in late January 2025, Trump signed an executive order to sanction the ICC over its investigations into top Israeli officials.
British barrister Karim Khan, who was the ICC's chief prosecutor, was the top sanctioned individual at the time.
He has since been removed through a vote by member states, albeit due to sexual misconduct allegations. Khan has denied them.
Three out of eight ICC judges were also sanctioned, alongside two of Khan's deputies, the United Nations special rapporteur for the occupied Palestinian territories, and three Palestinian human rights organisations.
The judges have since sued the Trump administration.
The Trump executive order followed a White House visit by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is wanted by the ICC over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Gaza since October 2023.
Netanyahu and his then defence minister, Yoav Gallant, were issued arrest warrants in November 2024, alongside three Hamas leaders, who have since been killed by Israel.
All non-US individuals and their family members who assist in ICC investigations into US citizens or allies fall under the sanctions order. Their assets are frozen, they cannot use the international banking system, and they cannot enter the US.
"The Trump Administration stands ready to take additional measures, if necessary, to systematically dismantle the ICC until it is incapable of threatening American sovereignty," Rubio said.

Migrant workers eligible for occupational accident legal aid: Ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
16:38:03 UTC
01:38:03 KST

Blue-collar migrant workers injured on the job are eligible for a Ministry of Labor (MOL) legal assistance program for occupational accident victims and can receive interpretation services throughout the process, the ministry told CNA Wednesday.
The confirmation came as the MOL is set to expand the program from Jan. 1, 2027, to provide legal representation during criminal trials in occupational accident cases, extending existing assistance beyond the investigation stage.
In a statement to CNA, the MOL said the program provides legal consultations, lawyers to accompany workers during settlement and mediation proceedings, and litigation assistance to occupational accident victims, including migrant workers.
Photo: CNA
For migrant workers, “interpretation services are provided throughout the process,” the ministry said.
The MOL has also instructed local government personnel dedicated to occupational accident cases to assess the needs of the migrant workers they assist and connect them with lawyers where necessary, according to the statement.
The statement came after CNA questioned MOL Department of Labor Relations Director-General Wang Hou-wei (王厚偉) at a news briefing Tuesday about migrant workers’ eligibility for the program and the availability of interpretation services.
Wang confirmed at the time that the assistance covers migrant workers, including live-in caregivers and domestic helpers who are not covered by Taiwan’s Labor Standards Act.
He also noted that interpretation services are particularly important for migrant workers, who “definitely need this kind of assistance; otherwise, they would have difficulty asserting many of their rights.”
Trial-stage assistance from 2027
The program’s expansion to cover criminal trials from Jan. 1, 2027 is intended to “fill a gap” in the current system by extending lawyers’ assistance beyond the investigation stage, said Legal Aid Foundation CEO Steven Chou (周漢 威), who also spoke at Tuesday’s briefing.
“We believe there should also be a lawyer alongside [the worker] during the trial,” said Chou, whose foundation works with the MOL on the program.
He said lawyers can help identify witnesses and other evidence, particularly because the prosecutor handling the case at trial may not be the same one who conducted the investigation and may be less familiar with the case.
Lawyers can also explain to the court the impact of an accident on workers and their families, including physical disabilities and psychological trauma, when judges consider sentencing, Chou said.
In addition, they can advise workers and their families during settlement negotiations and help them seek reasonable compensation from their employers, he added.
Information provided by the MOL showed that the program includes assistance with legal fees, up to NT $100,000 (US$3,129) per case for necessary expenses such as application fees, as well as living-expense assistance for eligible workers involved in litigation.
Chou told CNA that lawyers assigned through the foundation to handle occupational accident cases under the program are paid NT$20,000 for representing complainants during criminal investigations and NT$30,000 during trial proceedings.
Regarding the experience of its legal aid lawyers, Chou said the foundation had 4,889 such lawyers in 2025, with around 61 percent having practiced law for more than 11 years.
MOL data showed that Taiwan had 895,115 blue-collar migrant workers as of late June.

The promise of the Chinese market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
16:38:01 UTC
01:38:01 KST

For more than a decade, the debate surrounding China’s global economic expansion has largely revolved around one phrase: “debt-trap diplomacy.”
According to this narrative, Beijing deliberately extends unsustainable loans to developing countries and later exploits financial distress to secure strategic assets or political concessions. While some lending practices have raised legitimate concerns, evidence that China systematically uses debt to obtain strategic assets remains contested. Yet this debate has obscured a more important question: If debt is not the principal mechanism through which China expands its economic influence, what is?
Across the developing world, governments have sought closer economic ties with China based on an understandable assumption. The world’s second-largest economy, with a consumer market of more than 1.4 billion people, appears to offer extraordinary opportunities for exports, investment and industrial development. Even capturing a tiny fraction of Chinese demand could transform the economies of many smaller countries. Expanding trade with China has often been treated as a measure of economic success in itself.
Growing trade volumes do not necessarily translate into growing prosperity. Commodity exporters such as Chile and Brazil have benefited enormously from Chinese demand, but even in successful cases, exports often remain concentrated in a narrow range of raw materials while imports become increasingly diversified and technologically sophisticated.
In a growing number of developing economies, China’s trade relationships have become increasingly asymmetric. Chinese manufactured goods enter developing countries’ markets rapidly and competitively, while many of those countries struggle to gain meaningful access to China’s domestic market or diversify the products they sell there. Trade expands, but the economic benefits become unevenly distributed. Rather than producing more resilient economies, these relationships can increase dependence on Chinese manufacturing while limiting opportunities for domestic industrial development.
The problem is that governments frequently confuse trade volume with trade quality. Trade volume simply measures how much two countries exchange. Trade quality measures whether that relationship bolsters domestic productive capacity, diversifies exports, encourages technological upgrading and improves long-term economic resilience. Two countries can celebrate record bilateral trade while experiencing different economic outcomes.
During the past two decades, China has become one of Latin America’s largest trading partners. Chinese demand has created enormous opportunities for exporters of soybeans, copper, iron ore, lithium and other commodities. At the same time, Chinese manufacturers have dramatically expanded their presence across Latin American markets, supplying everything from consumer electronics and automobiles to machinery, textiles and household goods.
This growing commercial relationship has undoubtedly generated benefits. Consumers enjoy lower prices and greater product variety, while exporters of natural resources have gained access to one of the world’s largest markets. Yet beneath these impressive trade figures lies a more complicated reality.
Many Latin American economies continue exporting a relatively narrow range of commodities while importing increasingly sophisticated manufactured products from China. Instead of moving up the value chain, several countries have become more dependent on raw material exports and imported industrial goods.
When Honduras switched diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to the People’s Republic of China in 2023, officials emphasized China’s enormous market, promising new opportunities for agricultural exports, infrastructure investment and broader economic cooperation. Shrimp producers expected that access to Chinese consumers would compensate for the loss of Taiwan’s market.
Reality has proven far more challenging. Honduran shrimp exports failed to compensate for the loss of the Taiwanese market and negotiations toward a free-trade agreement have officially come to a halt, online investigative magazine Expediente Publico said.
Chinese manufactured imports also continue to expand their presence in the Honduran market. This demonstrates an important lesson: Diplomatic recognition alone does not guarantee commercial success.
Access to China’s market is often considerably more complex than governments initially anticipate. Asymmetry begins with market access. Chinese manufacturers can usually enter smaller markets relatively quickly. Smaller exporters often face a different reality.
Regulatory approvals, sanitary and phytosanitary standards, licensing procedures, technical requirements and distribution challenges can significantly delay or limit market access. At the same time, many developing economies lack the industrial capacity needed to compete effectively within China’s demanding domestic market, resulting in differences in industrial scale, logistics and regulatory capacity.
Unlike smaller economies that often liberalize imports relatively quickly, access to China’s domestic market frequently depends on lengthy regulatory approvals and administrative procedures that could delay or limit exports even after diplomatic agreements are signed.
As a result, imports frequently expand much faster than exports.
When Chinese manufactured products dominate domestic markets, local firms might struggle to compete on price. Consumers benefit from cheaper goods, but local manufacturers often face increasing pressure, particularly in sectors producing lower-value products.
A trade deficit does not automatically indicate unhealthy dependence. What matters is whether imports contribute to greater productive capacity or simply replace domestic manufacturing. This distinction between productive integration and passive dependence should shape how governments evaluate economic partnerships with China.
China would remain one of the world’s largest trading partners for decades to come, and few governments can afford to ignore the opportunities presented by its economy.
The more important question is whether those relationships promote long-term economic development.
The issue applies not only to Latin America, but also to countries across Africa, Southeast Asia and the Pacific.
As Beijing continues competing with Taipei for diplomatic recognition, access to China’s economy remains one of its most persuasive diplomatic arguments. However, governments should evaluate potential opportunities using measurable economic outcomes rather than optimistic projections.
Headline trade figures reveal how much countries trade, but not whether that trade strengthens their economies.
A healthier assessment would examine whether trade contributes to export diversification, stronger domestic industries, technological upgrades and greater resilience against external economic shocks. Those indicators provide a much clearer picture of whether economic engagement genuinely strengthens national development.
For years, policymakers have asked whether China creates dependence through debt. The more important question is whether dependence increasingly develops through trade itself.
Countries considering deeper economic engagement with China should ask a simple question: Would larger trade make their economies more productive, diversified and resilient, or simply more dependent on a larger trading partner?
Juan Fernando Herrera Ramos is a Honduran journalist based in Taipei. His work on Taiwan-China-Latin America relations has been published in Nikkei Asia, The Diplomat and the Taipei Times.
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

The group, led by former Polish prime minister Beata Szydlo, also met Legislative Yuan Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜), a gesture spanning Taiwan’s political divide. For most Taiwanese observers, this was a pleasant, if minor, diplomatic event. It was much more than that — and the timing matters. Within the same fortnight, Hudson Institute senior fellow Ken Moriyasu said in the Washington Examiner

Set to take effect from Sept. 15, the regulation expands the People’s Republic of China’s powers to restrict people from leaving the country in the name of “safeguarding national sovereignty, security and development interests.” International observers widely regard it as another step back to a closed China. Given Beijing’s insistence that Taiwan is “a part of China,” experts warn Taiwanese traveling to China of increasing risk of indefinite detainment. Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) Minister Chiu Chui-cheng (邱垂正) has likewise warned that China has repeatedly revised

Ministry details efforts on asphalt-related pollution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
16:38:01 UTC
01:38:01 KST

Up to 123 of the 127 asphalt mixing operators nationwide have upgraded their pollution control equipment under supervision by the Ministry of Environment’s Environmental Management Administration, achieving an improvement rate of 96.8 percent.
The ministry has revised and announced the Management Regulations for Facilities to Control Fugitive Dust Air Pollution from Stationary Pollution Sources (固定污染源逸散性粒狀污染物空氣污染防制設施管理辦法) to improve the overall air quality and resolve the issue of asphalt odor affecting local residents.
The administration’s northern, central and southern environmental management centers collaborated with local authorities on inspecting 127 asphalt mixing operators nationwide and required 125 of them to conduct fully enclosed operations or set up a local exhaust ventilation system.
Photo: Lee Wen-de, Taipei Times
The administration yesterday said that 123 operators made the improvements as required, achieving a completion rate of 96.8 percent.
For those who failed to improve their operations, the administration imposed 14 fines, amounting to a total of NT$995,000 (US$31,155), it said.
Article 7 of the revised act stipulates that asphalt mixing operators must be equipped with a local exhaust ventilation system with an efficiency of at least 60 percent, or conduct their operations in an enclosed environment, the administration said.
The new rule has been implemented from July 6, it said.
While up to 96.8 percent of the operators have improved their operations, some of them adopted advanced techniques to enhance their efforts, the administration said.
For example, some asphalt mixing plants adopted an enclosed unloading approach or installed curtain barriers to prevent the unloaded materials from spreading to the atmosphere, increasing the efficiency of exhaust ventilation, it said.
However, some operators were fined as they failed to abide by the law to install exhaust ventilation equipment, collect air pollutants, operate in compliance with the terms of their permits, maintain normal operation of their pollution control facilities, or report the generation and disposal of waste, the administration said.
Regarding the odor of recycled asphalt pavement, the administration said asphalt manufacturers must properly operate secondary combustion chambers — also known as waste gas incinerators — by preheating the chambers to 650°C or higher prior to production.
Processing, unloading and storage tank areas must be enclosed or have local exhaust ventilation systems to prevent the release of odors and volatile organic compounds, it said.
The plants that fail to complete the required improvements or installations would face fines of NT$100,000 to NT$20 million, with serious violations subject to suspension of projects or operations, or revocation of operating permits, it said.

CAR: Scores killed in landslide at illegal gold mine
August 19, 2026
Authorities in the western part of the Central African Republic (CAR) say dozens of laborers were killed Tuesday afternoon when a landslide buried them at the illegal Zamboye mining site near the Cameroon border — about 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the town of Baboua.
Death tolls have ranged from "at least 30" initially to "over 100," with local authorities saying the window for survival is quickly closing for the many miners still buried at the site.
Video uploaded to social media platforms showed bodies churning in earth as the landslide lunges into the open-pit site beneath, burying everything in its path.
Frantic rescue activities continued on Wednesday with reports of mud-covered young men and women pulling bodies from the mine's collapsed entrance, as still more screamed for help.
"The collapse of several underground tunnels in which miners were operating," was given as the cause of the collapse by the Baboua public prosecutor's office, which also announced that an investigation had been launched.
CAR government spokesman Evariste Ngamana expressed sympathy and pledged the government was "working hard to provide relief and assistance."
What is the state of CAR's 'artisanal' mines?
Improvised "artisanal" mines in the gold-rich region are often illegal and shoddily built, following limited or no safety standards whatsoever.
That means the thousands of laborers who use their hands to mine for gold every day, put their lives at risk each time they enter one.
Serious accidents are a regular occurrence and these are usually very deadly.
Dozens of miners have been killed in landslides in the area since the beginning of the year.

Some 11,000 residents remain in active combat zone in Donetsk Oblast, all children evacuated

Source: a Ukrainian news agency Ukrinform

Over half of US Jewish studies faculty records linked to anti-Israel positions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
16:37:32 UTC
01:37:32 KST

A new national faculty audit claimed that over 50 percent of audited university faculty members and related program files in Jewish Studies, Israel Studies, Hebrew language, and Holocaust and Genocide Studies were associated with documented anti-Israel public positions.
The study was conducted by The Olam, an institutional intelligence platform for Israel and the global Jewish economy, and published in early August. According to the report, the research analyzed 2,499 faculty members and institutional entries across 313 American universities, cross-referencing names and program listings against nine documented public petition campaigns and organizational records spanning from May 2021 through the spring of 2026.
Introducing the scope of the project, Ronn Torossian, publisher of The Olam, told The Jerusalem Post that the audit represents “the largest audit ever undertaken of Jewish Studies and Israel Studies faculties in the United States,” and said the report reveals that “more than half the professors in America teaching about Judaism, the Hebrew language, the State of Israel, and the history of the Holocaust have publicly positioned themselves against the Jewish state.”
Audit finds anti-Israel positions among faculty records
The research alleged that 1,298 of the analyzed entries, or 51.9%, featured documented anti-Israel public positions as defined by the study’s criteria. Among individual educators specifically identified as teaching in the relevant fields of Jewish, Israel, Hebrew, or Holocaust studies, the audit claimed that 401 out of 1,014, or 39.5%, held such positions
It reported particularly high concentrations at Ivy League universities, where Torossian noted that “72.3 percent of audited faculty records have documented anti-Israel positions.”
To establish these metrics, the study classified an anti-Israel stance based on specific public actions, such as leadership roles in groups like Faculty for Justice in Palestine (FSJP) or Jewish Voice for Peace (JVP), alongside signing petitions that endorsed academic boycotts, characterized Zionism as “settler colonialism,” labeled Israel an apartheid state, or defined its military actions as genocide.
The researchers noted that they deliberately excluded mainstream political criticisms – such as opposing specific government policies, advocating for a two-state solution, or demanding accountability for civilian casualties – that reflect ongoing debates within Israeli society itself.
“These professors are the people hired to teach the next generation about Judaism, the Hebrew language, the State of Israel, and the history of the Holocaust,” the report stated, arguing that the documented positions fell outside the consensus of mainstream Zionism.
Endowed chairs appear among petition signatories
The audit identified 14 holders of endowed chairs, positions funded by donors often intended to strengthen Jewish scholarship, who appeared among the signatories of these examined campaigns. Highlighting this aspect, Torossian pointed out that “14 endowed chairs – positions funded by Jewish philanthropists specifically to strengthen Jewish scholarship – are held by faculty openly opposed to Israel,” adding that donors established these funds to strengthen Jewish education. “Instead, many now fund scholars who describe Zionism as ‘settler colonialism,’ endorse academic boycotts of Israeli universities, and use language like ‘Jewish supremacy’ to describe the Jewish state.”
Beyond academic boycotts and political definitions, the evaluated petitions also encompassed broader advocacy, including protests against administrative discipline targeting pro-Palestinian organizers and pushback against the alleged weaponization of antisemitism claims
Furthermore, the report noted a significant escalation in petition activity. The March 2025 “Not in Our Name” letter, initiated by New England faculty and staff to protest campus crackdowns and the alleged weaponization of antisemitism claims, gathered over 3,400 academic signatures, becoming the largest single petition in the documented record.
How the faculty audit was conducted
The study’s methodology involved compiling rosters from publicly available university websites between July and August 2026, including every institutional member program of the Association for Jewish Studies and every US center or chair listed by the Association for Israel Studies. The researchers said that they matched faculty names to petition signatories using university affiliation, department, academic title, and full name.
They acknowledged limitations, noting that their audit captured only publicly available positions and did not account for faculty who may have held private views, nor did it capture Hebrew language instructors, who, they said, rarely signed political letters.
Addressing the implications of the data, Torossian said, “The question before Jewish families, donors, and institutional leaders is straightforward: Will we demand transparency about who teaches these subjects and what they publicly believe? Will endowments established to strengthen Jewish education actually accomplish that mission? The Olam created this study to answer these questions with data. The findings are now public. What institutions, families, and donors choose to do with this information is their decision.”

Thailand issues arrest warrants for 20 Israelis in sweeping Koh Samui business crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
16:37:17 UTC
01:37:17 KST

Thai police launched a sweeping operation against foreign business networks suspected of using Thai citizens as nominee shareholders to conceal foreign ownership of companies, land and restricted businesses, with arrest warrants issued for 20 Israelis on Koh Samui, Walla reported on Wednesday.
The Koh Samui Provincial Court issued warrants for the Israelis as part of the investigation, more than for citizens of any other foreign country included in the operation, excluding Thai nationals themselves.
Among the Israelis arrested was prominent real estate developer Gal Bieber, 45, who was detained on Saturday by officers from the Bo Phut Police Station and immigration police from Surat Thani Province.
According to police, Bieber is suspected of providing false information to public officials that led to false details being entered into official documents, unlawfully managing businesses restricted to Thai citizens, and using Thai citizens and corporations to conceal foreign ownership and management of businesses. At this stage, these remain allegations.
Thai police issue warrants for 20 Israelis in Koh Samui business crackdown
According to the suspicions made public, Gal and his wife, Roni, established a multilayered corporate structure and placed Thai citizens as shareholders in name only.
Authorities allege that the network of companies was used to operate an international school without a license and to purchase, hold, develop, sell and rent luxury villas, mainly to Israeli clients.
Thai authorities said a review of company records showed that one of the companies linked to the couple was initially registered under the names of Thai shareholders, with most of its shares transferred about a month later to Roni Bieber. The shareholders, directors, company capital and areas of business activity were subsequently changed repeatedly.
In total, authorities examined 12,906 companies registered on Koh Samui. Authorities found foreign shareholders in 8,254 of them, while 875 were flagged as having characteristics that could indicate the use of nominee shareholders.
After screening the information, the operation focused on 61 companies that held 42 plots of land and buildings spanning more than 53 dunams, valued at an estimated 1.5 billion baht, or approximately NIS 140 million.
Authorities opened 60 cases against 88 suspects, including 26 Thai citizens and 62 foreigners. Arrest warrants were issued for all 62 foreign suspects, including 20 Israelis, 17 Russians, 12 French nationals and two citizens each from Ukraine and Germany. Authorities said 27 suspects, including two Israelis, were arrested on the day of the operation.
During searches, police seized incorporation documents, accounting books, computers, mobile phones and digital information. Police said they would use the material to expand the investigation and identify additional individuals involved both inside and outside Thailand.
On Monday, two days after the Koh Samui operation, Israeli Ambassador to Thailand Dr. Alona Fisher-Kamm and members of the embassy delegation met Surat Thani Provincial Police commander Sawat Suksri and Tourist Police Division 3 commander Satasak Yimcharoen.
The meeting took place amid a rise in the number of Israelis on Koh Samui and nearby islands, recent tensions and friction between local residents and Israelis, and increased enforcement against businesses suspected of illegal activity.
The meeting also aimed to strengthen coordination, ensure the safety of Israeli tourists, and encourage responsible tourism in the country. The ambassador thanked police for assisting Israelis and said the overwhelming majority obey the law, while acknowledging that "there are also exceptional cases of improper behavior." She stressed that the embassy briefs Israelis traveling to Thailand on local laws, customs and culture.
She asked authorities to contact the embassy directly in any incident involving Israelis to enable a swift and coordinated response. Thai authorities, for their part, said they enforce the law transparently and equally against everyone, regardless of nationality.
The Koh Samui operation is the seventh stage of a Thai government campaign against concealed foreign control of land and businesses in tourist areas. During the previous six stages, authorities examined 238 companies and 272 plots of land across seven provinces, including Phuket, Krabi, Phang Nga and Chonburi. So far, authorities have issued 178 arrest warrants as part of the operations, and 91 suspects have been arrested.
Roni Bieber: "All our actions were accompanied by a Thai lawyer and accountant"
Roni Bieber told Walla, "We reject the claims raised against us. The businesses were established and operated with the guidance of local professionals and with the intention of complying with the requirements of Thai law. This was not a case of using nominee shareholders, and all the partners involved are real people who were part of the business activity.
"We are cooperating fully with the authorities through our lawyers and are providing all the required documents and information. Gal reported as required and has been released on bail while the legal proceedings are underway.
"Since the matter is currently under examination and in legal proceedings, we cannot address every detail, but we believe the facts will become clear and our names will be cleared. We respect Thai law and the authorities. All our actions were accompanied by a Thai lawyer and accountant who told him how to do everything and accompanied us when the companies were opened and the businesses were established. We placed our full trust in them and did as they instructed, but when the law changed, they disappeared and took no responsibility, and because they are Thai, they are free from law enforcement.
"We ask that partial information or premature conclusions not be published before the examination is completed."

Fuel stations in Moscow have reimposed limits on gasoline purchases due to fuel shortages linked to Ukrainian drone attacks on refineries and strong seasonal demand, according to Reuters witnesses and fuel suppliers.
Shortages began to gather pace in May and had spread to most Russian regions by July, but fuel stations in Moscow were able to ease an earlier wave of restrictions in June.
Ukraine has targeted Russian oil refineries in an effort to undermine Moscow's war effort and reduce energy revenues.
To boost domestic supplies, Russian authorities have banned exports of gasoline and diesel, eased fuel quality requirements and began importing petroleum products.
Reuters witnesses also saw long queues at some filling stations in Moscow and the surrounding region.
Gasoline purchases restricted to 40 liters per customer in Russia
A customer hotline operator at Gazprom Neft SIBN.MM said gasoline and diesel sales at the company's automated filling stations in Moscow were limited to 40 liters per customer.
At Gazprom Neft's other filling stations, diesel sales remain unrestricted, while gasoline purchases are capped at 60 liters per vehicle.
Rosneft ROSN.MM, Russia's largest oil producer, said gasoline sales at all its filling stations across Russia were limited to 30 liters per vehicle, while diesel sales faced no restrictions.
The company also warned customers of longer waiting times because of heightened demand.
Lukoil LKOH.MM said it had introduced fuel sales restrictions in Moscow and the surrounding region because of elevated demand, unscheduled refinery maintenance and the need to ensure stable operations at its filling stations.
It did not disclose the specific limits.
Tatneft's TATN.MM customer hotline said gasoline sales at its filling stations were limited to 50 liters per vehicle.

A UK court was told during trial proceedings at Kingston Crown Court that Tony Greenstein, a prominent Jewish anti-Zionist activist and founding member of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, issued a rallying cry inviting support for Hamas.
Local UK media reports outlined that the charges stem from three posts published on Greenstein’s X/Twitter account on October 7, 2023, the day of the Hamas-led attack on Israel, which prosecutors argued breached the Terrorism Act 2000 by intentionally encouraging support for a proscribed terrorist organization.
Prosecutors point to Greenstein's October 7 posts
Legal representatives detailed the contents of the posts on Tuesday, during the court hearings, pointing to specific messaging where Greenstein allegedly wrote, “Please share. Full support for the Gaza ghetto uprising.” Prosecutors said that the posts also contained links to a blog which included the line, “The time to fight is now. Whatever criticisms one can make of Hamas, we should congratulate them on this well-planned and audacious attack on the Zionist enemy."
During the hearing, prosecutor Kate Temple-Mabe said that although Greenstein did not explicitly name Hamas in his X posts, his reference to the “‘Gaza ghetto uprising’ – in that specific context, on that specific date – can only have meant support for Hamas.” Prosecutors maintained that his language went beyond political dissent, representing a “clear invitation of moral or intellectual support” for a proscribed organization.
Defense argues posts were political expression
Greenstein’s defense counsel contested the allegations and said that the statements formed part of broader anti-Zionist political expression, legitimate commentary, and analysis regarding the Middle East conflict rather than an invitation to unlawful terrorist support..
During his police interview, it was noted that Greenstein indicated he did not support everything Hamas stands for, and his lawyers argue that the words used were not intended as an invitation of support.
Greenstein, a 72-year-old activist and writer, has a history of political controversy, including his expulsion from the Labour Party in 2018 over allegations of antisemitism and a subsequent suspended prison sentence in September 2023 for an action targeting an Israeli defense contractor.
Campaign Against Antisemitism responds to trial
A spokesperson for Campaign Against Antisemitism said in a statement to The Jerusalem Post, “Tony Greenstein has long courted controversy, and indeed one of his better-known interventions came when he sued us for labeling him a ‘notorious antisemite.’ His libel claim against us humiliatingly backfired after the High Court ruled it was permissible for us to describe him as such. Any alleged support for a terrorist organization is a serious charge, and we are following the case closely.”
The trial continues as the court examines the specific wording of the contested posts and the broader context in which they were disseminated.
